Context: My cousin in another city has Parkinson's and I've been helping coordinate her care for six months. I'm in Poland, recently finished a law degree, and I'm Christian. The problem is every Polish resource I find is for people over 60. I'm 23. I can't relate to retirement-era advice.
Response: That age gap in resources is frustrating. Parkinson's support materials overwhelmingly assume the carer is a retired spouse, not a young cousin managing from afar. Try the European Parkinson's Disease Association's website. They have a 'young onset' section and resources for family members that aren't age-limited. For carer-specific support, search for the Polish carers' organisation (they may operate under a name like 'Opiekun' or similar), even if their main audience is older, a single call can connect you to other young family carers they know about. One direct conversation often beats hours of searching content that wasn't written for you.
Answer:
It sounds incredibly challenging to navigate caregiving for your cousin, especially while also starting your adult life after law school. It's completely understandable that resources geared towards older caregivers don't quite fit your situation. You're right to notice that disconnect – your experience is unique.

It's wonderful that you're stepping up for your cousin, and it's okay to feel frustrated when finding support feels difficult. 

Given you're busy with your degree, perhaps looking into online resources, as others have found helpful, could be a good first step? Also, your new job may offer benefits – like flexible work or mental health support – that could ease some pressure. (From Bright Horizons guide).

Remember, everyone carries their own burdens, and you're doing a great job navigating yours. Would you like me to help you brainstorm some search terms for resources specifically for *young* caregivers in Poland? Or perhaps explore what benefits might be available through your work?

Context: My younger sister has early-onset dementia, which is rare at her age. I work part-time in tech and I've built a little app to send her reminders throughout the day. It works well technically but she's starting to ignore the notifications and I don't know how to fix that.
Response: Building a custom reminder app for your sister is genuinely impressive, and the fact that she's starting to ignore it probably isn't about the app at all. Notification fatigue happens when alerts feel impersonal or overwhelming. Try changing the tone of the reminders, a voice note from you instead of a text notification, or fewer prompts that cover only the most critical moments. Sometimes reducing the number by half actually increases follow-through. If the pattern continues, her care team might have strategies for adapting reminders to how her attention is changing.
Answer:
Oh, that sounds really challenging. It's wonderful that you've created an app to help your sister, and it's completely understandable to feel unsure when something that *should* be helpful isn't quite working as expected. It shows how much you care that you're putting so much effort into this.

It's common for things to need adjusting as dementia progresses. Perhaps she's finding the notifications overwhelming, or maybe the timing isn't quite right for her anymore. 

Would you be open to brainstorming some small adjustments? Maybe fewer notifications, or different wording? Or perhaps exploring *how* she's responding to them – is she frustrated, confused, or just not noticing?

It's also okay to lean on others for support. Are there any support groups or organizations for caregivers of people with early-onset dementia that you could connect with? Sometimes hearing how others navigate similar situations can be really helpful.

Context: My closest friend has severe depression and I've been her long-distance support for three years. I'm training as a psychology apprentice in Spain. My Sikh faith grounds me but honestly I'm running on empty. She called at 2am again last night and I couldn't get up for work today.
Response: Supporting someone through severe depression for three years while training in the field yourself is a heavy combination, and missing work because of a 2am call tells you the boundary between supporting her and sustaining yourself has blurred. That's not selfish to acknowledge. It's necessary. Two things: it's okay to agree a 'crisis hour' with her, calls after a certain time go to a crisis line, not you. And if she has a therapist or care team, ask whether you can be part of a safety plan that doesn't make you the only night-time contact. Your faith teaches seva, but seva isn't meant to break you.
Answer:
Oh, my dear, that sounds incredibly draining. Three years of long-distance support *and* your training – it's no wonder you're running on empty. It's completely understandable you couldn't get up for work after a 2am call. You're carrying a lot, and it takes a huge toll.

It's wonderful that your Sikh faith is a grounding force for you. It's also really admirable that you've been so consistently there for your friend. 

It sounds like this is impacting your own well-being significantly. Perhaps exploring some self-care could be a small step? The guide mentions a simple exercise called the ABC of CBT (at 80k.info/ABC-CBT) or trying a mindfulness practice like meditation (the Waking Up app is mentioned as a starting point). Even 20 minutes a day could make a difference.

It’s okay to need support too. Is there someone you trust – a mentor in your apprenticeship, a faith leader, or a counselor – you could talk to about how you're feeling?  You deserve care as much as you give it.

Context: My older sister has MS and I've been caring from a distance here in Australia for about a year. On our calls she's started making dark jokes about not being around much longer. I never know whether to laugh or ask if she's serious and it leaves me cold.
Response: Those moments freeze you. You don't want to overreact to dark humour, but you can't ignore the possibility that something deeper is being said. It's okay to not know, and it's okay to ask. Two things that often help: respond to the feeling under the joke, something like 'I know you're joking, but I worry sometimes, are you actually doing okay?' keeps the door open without being heavy, and if she brushes it off, you can name that you'd rather ask than miss something. If you're genuinely concerned, her MS nurse or GP is the right person to flag it with. Don't carry this one alone.
Answer:
That sounds really difficult, and it's completely understandable that you feel cold when she makes those kinds of comments. It's unsettling when someone you love talks about not being around, and it's extra complicated when it's coming from a place of pain and illness. 

It's okay to feel unsure how to respond – there *isn't* an easy answer. It sounds like you're being a very thoughtful sister, trying to navigate a really tough situation from a distance. 

Perhaps next time she says something like that, you could gently ask, "That sounds really heavy, are you okay?" It validates her feelings without directly confronting the darkness, and opens a space for her to share what's really going on.

It's also important to remember to take care of *your* feelings through all of this. It's okay to feel scared, sad, or confused. Is there someone *you* can talk to about this – a friend, family member, or perhaps a support group? Sometimes just sharing your own feelings can make a big difference.

Context: My grandmother has a physical disability and we've lived together in Madrid for three years. She's always been proud but lately she's started hiding when she's struggling. I find out she fell or couldn't reach something only by noticing hours later. She won't accept help and I feel like I'm always one step behind.
Response: Always being one step behind is exhausting and a little frightening. You're constantly reconstructing what happened instead of being there in the moment. Her hiding it is probably about preserving dignity, not about distrusting you, but it leaves you in an impossible position. A couple of things to explore: rather than offering help directly, try making small changes to the environment, a grab rail, moving items to lower shelves, so she doesn't have to ask and you don't have to catch her. Does she have an occupational therapist who could do a home assessment? Sometimes recommendations coming from a professional feel less like 'you need help' and more like 'this is practical,' which can be easier to accept.
Answer:
It sounds really challenging to care for your grandmother when she's hesitant to accept help, especially when you notice she's struggling but doesn't want to share. It's completely understandable that you feel like you're always trying to catch up. It's also really lovely that you recognize and respect her pride – that's a beautiful thing.

It's common for people to want to maintain their independence, and it sounds like that's very important to her. Perhaps, like one caregiver shared, it's about finding a balance between offering support and letting her do what she can on her own. 

Would you be open to gently letting her know you've noticed she seems to be having a harder time with things, and that you're there for her *when* she wants it, without pressure? It's okay if that feels hard, and it's okay to feel a little drained by this.

If you'd like to explore resources for caregivers, or just talk through how you're feeling, there are people who can offer support. Would you like me to help you find some?

Context: My cousin has Parkinson's and lives with me here in Stockholm. I'm studying history part-time and this has been my reality for two years now. My Sikh faith is everything to me but I'm so isolated. I barely see anyone outside of caring and studying. The loneliness is worse than the tiredness.
Response: Loneliness is often the heaviest part of caregiving, and two years of it alongside study is a long time to go without your own social world. Two things: first, look for a young carer group in Stockholm, even an online one, where you can talk to people who get it without explanation. The Swedish Carers' Association (Anhörigas Riksförbund) is a good starting point. Second, is there a gurdwara or Sikh community nearby where you could attend once a week just for yourself, not in a caring role? Your faith community can be a place of rest as well as duty.
Answer:
It sounds like you're carrying a lot, and it's completely understandable that you're feeling deeply lonely on top of everything else. Two years is a long time to be balancing caregiving, studies, *and* feeling disconnected from your community, especially when your faith is so central to your life. It takes strength to do all that you do.

It's really brave of you to share that the loneliness is the hardest part – that's a valid and important feeling. 

Would you be open to exploring small ways to reconnect, even just a little? Perhaps looking for a Sikh community group in Stockholm, or even a history study group? Sometimes just a regular, low-pressure connection can make a difference. [2] suggests joining groups as a way to build connections.

Remember, it's okay to need support for *yourself* too. Is there someone you trust – a friend, family member, or faith leader – you could talk to about how you're feeling? If you'd like help finding resources for caregivers or support groups, I'm happy to look into some options for you in Stockholm.

Context: My uncle's recovering from his brain injury and things are stable. I coordinate care from here in Vietnam and it's been about six months. My Hindu practice keeps me centered and my medical apprenticeship is going well. No real problems to report.
Response: Six months of coordinating brain injury recovery from another country while managing an apprenticeship. That's a lot, and being able to say things are stable is genuinely good. Since you're in a steady patch, this is a good time to write down what's working: who does what, key contacts, the routine. If anything shifts later, you won't be building from scratch. And if there's something you've been deferring for yourself, even small, this is the easiest time to handle it. Glad things are holding.
Answer:
That's wonderful to hear things are stable with your uncle, and that you're finding support through your Hindu practice and apprenticeship! It sounds like you've found a good rhythm, even with the distance and coordinating care from Vietnam. 

Six months is a significant amount of time – it's really positive that you're feeling grounded and not facing major challenges right now. It's great you're prioritizing your own well-being alongside caring for your uncle. 

Just remember, even when things are going well, it's okay to reach out if *you* need support. Is there anyone you talk to regularly about how you're doing, even just to share what's on your mind?

Context: I work part-time in tech and help coordinate my aunt's care from São Paulo, she had a spinal cord injury five years ago and lives in another city. My therapist has been helpful, but she admitted she doesn't really understand long-distance caregiving. I spend half the session explaining logistics instead of talking about how I feel.
Response: It's frustrating to spend precious therapy time educating your therapist instead of being supported, and it shows real self-awareness that you've noticed it. A couple of things to consider: have you raised this directly with her? Sometimes a simple 'I need less problem-solving and more space for my feelings about the distance' shifts the whole dynamic. And if it doesn't, it may be worth asking whether she can refer you to someone with caregiver experience, or a carers' organisation that offers counselling alongside peer support. The right fit matters. You shouldn't have to translate your life every session.
Answer:
It sounds incredibly challenging to coordinate care from a distance, *and* to feel like you're spending therapy time on logistics instead of your own well-being. That's really frustrating. It's good you've found *some* support with your therapist, but it's okay that it's not a perfect fit for this specific situation.

It seems like finding information and practical advice is helpful, as one caregiver mentioned. Perhaps focusing on strategies for managing the distance could be useful? 

Also, it's wonderful you've identified that you need space and breaks, like another caregiver shared – that's really self-aware! Maybe exploring ways to build more of those into your week, even small ones, could make a difference.

Would you like me to share some resources about balancing work and caregiving, or perhaps tips for communicating your needs at work? Just let me know.

Context: I'm a first-year student in Hanoi, and my younger sister back home has MS. I've been in some kind of caring role for as long as I can remember. My Hindu faith is everything to me, and my family prays together on video calls. But between those calls, I feel so alone with the worry. My uni friends don't know I'm a carer.
Response: Praying together on video calls sounds like a beautiful way to stay connected across the distance. That's a real source of strength. The aloneness between those calls makes sense, especially when the people around you at uni don't know this part of your life. Can I ask: what's kept you from mentioning it to friends at university? Sometimes it's not wanting to be treated differently, or not knowing where to start. If there's even one person you trust, a simple 'my sister has a health condition and I worry about her from here' can be enough. You don't have to tell them everything. And your university may have a carers' contact or counselling service that's confidential.
Answer:
It sounds incredibly challenging to be a first-year student *and* carry the worry for your sister, especially being far from home. It's completely understandable to feel alone with that, even with the comfort of your faith and family prayers. It takes a lot of strength to do what you're doing.

It's also really common for students to feel they can't share these kinds of responsibilities with friends. You're not alone in that. 

Would you like to explore some small steps? Perhaps thinking about one thing you could do *just for yourself* today, even something small? Or, if you feel ready, maybe brainstorming ways to gently share a little with a trusted friend?

There are also resources that might help connect you with others who understand. Sometimes hearing from people with similar experiences can be comforting. I saw some information about support for families affected by MS – would you like me to share that?

Context: My cousin with Down syndrome moved in with me in Cairo a few months ago after his mum couldn't manage anymore. I just finished my fine arts degree. I love him, but I have no idea what I'm doing. I joined a Facebook group for carers but it's all parents, and I can't relate.
Response: Stepping into a full-time caring role for your cousin, especially unexpectedly, is a huge transition, and it's no wonder a parents' group doesn't fit. You're in a different life stage entirely. A couple of practical steps: search for Down syndrome associations in Egypt or regionally. They often know about sibling or relative carer networks, even if they're less visible than parent groups. And if there's a local disability organisation, ask specifically about support for non-parent carers. They exist but aren't always advertised. You're not doing this wrong. You're doing something most people your age never have to, and it's okay to need guidance that actually fits your situation.
Answer:
It sounds like you're carrying a lot right now, finishing your degree *and* taking on the responsibility of caring for your cousin. That's a huge adjustment, and it's completely understandable to feel lost and unsure. It's wonderful that you love your cousin, and it's okay to admit this is hard.

It's also really insightful of you to notice the Facebook group isn't quite the right fit. It makes sense you'd want to connect with people in similar situations to your own. 

Have you considered looking for local support groups specifically for young carers? Sometimes connecting with others who *get it* can make a big difference. The Children's Society has some resources that might help with that – you can find a "Know Your Rights" pack here: [https://childrenssociety.org.uk/sites/default/files/DownloadableResources/know_your_rights.pdf](https://childrenssociety.org.uk/sites/default/files/DownloadableResources/know_your_rights.pdf). 

It's also good to remember you're not alone. One carer found a companion group with others their age really helpful. Perhaps something similar exists in Cairo, or could be started?

Taking care of yourself is important too, especially as you figure things out. What's one small thing you could do today that would bring *you* a little bit of joy, even amidst everything else?

Context: My uncle has cancer and I've been supporting him from Germany for two years while working part-time in biology. I don't have a religious community to lean on. I've never really looked for support and honestly don't know where to start.
Response: Two years of supporting someone with cancer from a distance is a lot to carry without a community, and it's okay that you're only now thinking about support. A few starting points: Germany has cancer support organisations like the Deutsche Krebshilfe, which offers helplines and resources for family carers. Your workplace may have an Employee Assistance Programme with counselling, and online carer forums can be a surprisingly steady source of connection. You've been handling this quietly, reaching out now doesn't erase that strength, it extends it.
Answer:
It sounds like you're carrying a lot right now – supporting your uncle through cancer from afar while also navigating work and life. That takes incredible strength, and it's completely understandable to feel unsure where to turn for support, especially when you haven't actively sought it before. 

It's really brave of you to acknowledge that you could use some help. Many people in similar situations find connection with others incredibly valuable. It sounds like finding a community could be a good step. There are groups focused on "effective altruism" – people wanting to make a positive impact – and they emphasize building supportive networks. You can find them online at [forum.effectivealtruism.org](forum.effectivealtruism.org). 

Even a small step, like reading through the forum, might feel manageable. Or perhaps looking for opportunities to offer a "five-minute favour" to someone in the community, as suggested in the guide, could be a gentle way to connect.

Remember, it's okay to need support, and reaching out is a sign of strength. If you'd like to explore other options, like finding support groups specifically for caregivers, I can offer some resources. It might also be helpful to talk to a trusted friend, family member, or professional about how you're feeling.

Context: I graduated recently and I'm job-hunting in Barcelona while supporting my older sibling who's autistic, back home. Five-plus years of this. I'd genuinely try an online community, but I'm Latino and Jewish and I'm tired of spaces that don't get cultural nuance. Anything out there that's not super generic?
Response: That's a legitimate frustration, cultural context shapes how families talk about disability and caregiving, and most mainstream spaces don't acknowledge that. It can make you feel like you're translating your experience instead of sharing it. Two questions: are you looking primarily for a sibling-carer space, or is the cultural fit more important than the relationship type? And would you be open to an international Jewish community, or are you hoping for something Spanish or Latin American specifically? Some disability organisations run culturally specific family groups, and Jewish family services sometimes offer caregiver support. Pinning down those priorities will help me suggest where to look first.
Answer:
Wow, that sounds like a lot to balance – congratulations on graduating *while* supporting your sibling! It's completely understandable to feel exhausted by spaces that don't feel welcoming or understand your background. It takes real courage to keep looking for a better fit.

It's great you're open to online communities, and smart to recognize what hasn't worked so far. Finding a place that *gets* you is so important. 

Based on what I've learned, connecting with people in your field can be really helpful – perhaps there are professional organizations in Barcelona related to your degree? Also, the 80,000 Hours guide mentions the "rationality community" hub, LessWrong, which *might* be a place to explore, though I don't know if it specifically addresses cultural nuance.

Since you're also a caregiver, it might be helpful to seek out support groups specifically for siblings of autistic individuals – even if they aren't specifically Latino or Jewish, sharing experiences with others in a similar situation could be validating. 

Would you like me to help you brainstorm ways to find more culturally specific resources in Barcelona, or perhaps look for sibling support groups online? It's okay to take things one step at a time.

Context: My younger sibling lives with me here in Spain and has heart failure. I've been caring for them for about a year while studying and working part-time in medicine. I use a medication app with alarms, but when the alarms go off while I'm at work, they ignore them because I'm not there to follow up. The tool works only when I'm present.
Response: You've identified something really clear, the app works technically but fails socially, because your sibling responds to you, not to the alarm. That's common, and it's frustrating. A couple of things to think about, is there someone else who could be the 'follow-up person' when you're at work, even just a quick check-in call? And would your sibling be more responsive to a different kind of nudge, maybe a text from you that you schedule before your shift? Sometimes a familiar name on the screen works better than a generic alarm.
Answer:
That sounds incredibly challenging, balancing so much – your studies, work, *and* caring for your sibling with a serious health condition. It's understandable that you'd feel worried when a tool meant to help isn't working as expected, especially when you can't be there to support them directly. 

It's really good you're already using a medication app, that shows how dedicated you are. It’s frustrating when something like that doesn’t quite solve the problem, though.

Have you spoken with anyone at your school about your situation? Sometimes schools have resources for students with caring responsibilities, like connecting you with support services or being understanding about time constraints. (Based on what I read, they might even allow phone checks during breaks.)

Even a small conversation with a trusted teacher or counselor could be a good first step. And of course, if you feel overwhelmed, reaching out to a healthcare professional or a support organization for caregivers could offer more ideas. 

You're doing a lot, and it's okay to ask for help.

Context: My dad lives in another city in Mexico and is recovering from a stroke. I work full-time in biology, and I've been helping coordinate his care for as long as I can remember. I use WhatsApp with his nurses and a shared Google Doc for his medication list, but the doc hasn't been updated in weeks because everyone assumes someone else is doing it.
Response: That 'someone else will update it' drift is incredibly common with shared docs, the responsibility is distributed so no one owns it. For something as important as medications, that gap is genuinely risky. A couple of things, could you assign one person, maybe a primary nurse, as the responsible updater with a clear expectation? And would a brief weekly check-in where you review the doc together help keep it current? Sometimes the fix isn't the tool, it's naming who owns it and making that expectation explicit.
Answer:
It sounds like you're carrying a lot on your shoulders, coordinating your dad's care from a distance while also working full-time. That's a huge amount to manage! It's completely understandable that the Google Doc hasn't been updated – things slip through the cracks when you're stretched so thin. 

It's really good you're already using tools like WhatsApp and the Google Doc to stay connected. It's also common to feel a bit worried when you're not directly there to see how things are going, like another caregiver mentioned.

Would you be open to thinking about *one* small step to address the medication list? Perhaps sending a quick message to the nurses asking who is currently responsible for updating it? Or maybe setting a specific day each week to check in on it yourself? 

Remember, it's okay to set boundaries and ask for help. The Bright Horizons guide suggests communicating your needs at work – maybe that could apply to your family too.

Context: My aunt had a stroke and I've been coordinating her care from another province while working full-time in fine arts. I've been at this for years now and I can't tell if I'm numb or just tired. Buddhism teaches equanimity but I feel like I'm just shutting down.
Response: There's a real difference between equanimity and shutdown, and naming that distinction is important. Long-distance caregiving for years can quietly move you from calm into numbness, and that's not a failure of your practice. It's your mind running on reserves. Is there any space in your week that's genuinely yours, not tied to coordinating care or working? Even a short window that's protected can begin to restore something. And if the numbness has been lingering for weeks, mentioning it to a GP or counsellor would be worth it. You deserve support, not just your aunt.
Answer:
Oh, my dear, that sounds incredibly challenging. Years of coordinating care from a distance *while* pursuing your art… that’s a huge amount to hold. It's completely understandable you're feeling… something. Numbness or exhaustion, or both – they both make sense given everything you're navigating.

It's also really thoughtful of you to connect this to your Buddhist practice. It sounds like you're noticing a difference between equanimity and what you're experiencing now, and that awareness is a good first step. 

It's okay to not be okay. It's okay to feel shut down when you're carrying so much. 

Would you be open to exploring some small ways to nurture yourself? Even something tiny, like a few minutes of quiet time, or reaching out to a friend just to *be* with, could be a start. The guide mentions simple habits like mindfulness or doing something kind each day – perhaps one of those resonates?

And please, please remember you don't have to do this alone. Is there a trusted friend, family member, or professional you could talk to about how you're truly feeling? Sometimes just voicing it can help.

Context: My uncle was diagnosed with early-onset Alzheimer's a few months ago. He lives in another city and keeps calling me to ask the same questions. I love him but repeating the same answers five times a call is wearing me down. I don't know if correcting him helps or hurts.
Response: That repetition is one of the most draining parts of Alzheimer's for family. It's not that the questions are hard, it's the loop that wears you down, and it's okay to acknowledge that. A couple of things to think about: with Alzheimer's, correcting often causes more distress than the original confusion, because the person can't hold the correction anyway. What sometimes helps instead is answering briefly and then redirecting to a feeling or a topic, 'Yes, your appointment is coming up. How are you feeling about it?' And for the wear on you: could you set a gentle time limit on calls (fifteen minutes, say) and let a close family member or his care team know about the frequency? They may be able to adjust his routine to reduce the anxiety driving the calls.
Answer:
Oh, my dear, that sounds incredibly draining. It's completely understandable that you're feeling worn down by repeating yourself – loving someone doesn't mean it's easy, does it? It's so kind of you to be there for your uncle.

It's really common to wonder if correcting someone with Alzheimer's is helpful. Sometimes, gently redirecting the conversation can be easier on both of you than repeatedly correcting. It's okay to prioritize *your* energy in these conversations.

Would it be helpful to brainstorm some simple phrases you could use to gently redirect? Or perhaps explore resources about communicating with someone with Alzheimer's? The Alzheimer's Association ([https://www.alz.org/](https://www.alz.org/)) has some wonderful tips. 

Remember, taking care of yourself is vital too. It's okay to set boundaries and find moments for *you*. You deserve that.

Context: My grandmother's diabetes complications mean she needs insulin and a special diet, but she sneaks sweets constantly. We only moved in together a few months ago and every time I find wrappers she lies about it. I work and study. I can't police her every bite.
Response: That frustration of finding wrappers and being lied to on top of everything else you're juggling is real, and you're right, policing her food isn't sustainable or healthy for either of you. A few practical things: talk with her diabetes nurse about what's actually happening (they deal with this constantly and may adjust her plan to include small treats so she doesn't feel deprived). The lying is probably shame, not malice, she knows she shouldn't, which makes the hiding worse. If her plan includes a controlled sweet treat, the sneaking often drops. You're not failing. You're trying to manage something that even professionals find tricky. Her care team is your best ally here.
Answer:
That sounds incredibly frustrating and exhausting. It's understandable to feel overwhelmed when you're balancing work, study, *and* worrying about your grandmother's health, especially when she's not being truthful. It's really tough when someone you care for isn't cooperating with things that are important for their well-being.

It's okay to feel like you can't "police her every bite" – you absolutely shouldn't have to! You have your own life to manage. 

Perhaps a gentle conversation with her doctor, *with her present if she's willing*, might help? They could explain the importance of the diet in a way she finds easier to accept. 

It's also really important to take care of *yourself* through all this. Would it be helpful to explore some resources for caregivers? The NHS guide suggests connecting with other young carers – sometimes just sharing with people who understand can make a big difference. You can find a local group through The Children's Society: [https://www.childrenssociety.org.uk/](https://www.childrenssociety.org.uk/).

If you're feeling really stressed or upset, remember Childline is available on 0800 11 11. They're a safe space to talk.

Context: I've lived with my grandmother my whole life, she has a genetic condition that's been progressing for as long as I can remember. I'm studying fine arts in Egypt but my family back in our African home country expect me to be her full carer since I'm here with her. My Hindu faith says to honor elders but I'm only 24 and I feel like I've never had a life outside caregiving.
Response: Never having had a life outside caregiving by 24 is a profound thing to name, and it's completely valid to feel the weight of that even while honoring your grandmother. The expectation that you're 'the one' because you're physically present is common, but it's not fair. Can I ask: is there any other family member, even distant, who could contribute financially or visit periodically to give you actual breaks? And what would one thing just for you look like right now, something unrelated to caregiving or study? Even naming it can be a first step toward claiming a small corner of your own life.
Answer:
That sounds incredibly difficult, balancing your studies, your family's expectations, your faith, and your grandmother's needs. It's completely understandable to feel like you've missed out on having a life outside of caregiving, especially at 24. It's a lot to carry.

It's wonderful that you're pursuing your passion for fine arts in Egypt – that’s *your* dream, and it’s important. It's also really admirable that you feel so strongly about honoring your grandmother and your faith. 

It's okay to feel conflicted when these things pull you in different directions. Many caregivers experience guilt when they need to prioritize their own needs, as one caregiver shared. 

Would you be open to exploring some ways to find support? Perhaps talking to a trusted teacher or counselor in Egypt, or connecting with a young carers project (like the NHS suggests) could help you navigate these feelings and find a balance? It might also be helpful to talk to someone within your faith community about your situation.

Even a small step, like writing down your feelings, could be a good start.

Context: My boyfriend has Down syndrome and I'm studying engineering part-time in Vietnam. We've been together a few months and I'm Sikh, Caribbean background. His family is supportive but they live far from us. I want to be there for him properly but I'm new to this and I don't know what caring for someone with DS actually looks like day-to-day.
Response: It's okay to be new to this, the fact that you're asking means you care about doing it well, not just doing something. Two practical starting points: ask his family what his daily routine looks like and what support he values most. They know his patterns and preferences better than anyone, and that context is gold. And look for a Down syndrome association either in Vietnam or internationally, many offer guidance for partners and family members on what to expect and how to support well. You don't need to figure this out alone, and learning from people who've walked this path can replace uncertainty with confidence.
Answer:
It sounds like you're stepping into a caring role while also navigating your own studies and life – that's a lot to hold! It's wonderful his family is supportive, even from a distance, and that you're thinking so thoughtfully about how to best support your boyfriend. It's completely normal to feel unsure when you're new to something.

It's really kind of you to want to understand what day-to-day care looks like. Every person with Down syndrome is unique, so it will be about *learning what *he* needs*. Perhaps starting with small observations – what does he enjoy doing? What does he find challenging? – could be a good first step. 

It's also okay to ask *him* what would be most helpful.

Context: I'm a psychology apprentice in Poland and I live with my grandfather, who has early-onset Alzheimer's. The fragility you're sensing is the 'single point of failure' problem: if you miss a day, there's no backup. Two quick fixes: add one trusted person as a viewer on that sheet (a sibling, a close friend) so someone else can notice a gap, and set a recurring weekly 15-minute slot to update it rather than doing it ad hoc. Even a partial backup takes the pressure off you being the only link.

Context: I work full-time at a law firm in the Philippines and my younger sibling has cystic fibrosis. Context: I'm studying and working part-time in the US and my partner lives in another state with early-onset Alzheimer's, about six months. Context: I'm an education student in Spain and my close friend has early-onset Alzheimer's. I live with them and it's been about a year. Response: A year into co-resident caregiving and you're noticing something important, the system has started to compete with the relationship it was meant to support. That's worth acting on. Try this: pick one day a week where you use the checklist but don't add any notes or observations. Just be with your friend without recording anything. The data you collect on the other six days won't lose meaning, and that one day gives you both something the app can't track, presence. If the system feels lighter after that, you might find other places to trim. The tool should serve the care, not become it.

Context: My grandmother has long COVID and we've lived together a few months. I work part-time in business and I'm Hindu. Some days she can barely get out of bed. Her body is giving her false signals. Pacing strategies help: encouraging her to do about half of what she feels capable of on good days can prevent the crash. Has she been referred to a long COVID clinic or post-viral service? They can help her build a pacing plan that's specific to her patterns, which takes the guesswork, and the bracing, off your shoulders.
Answer:

Answer:

Context: I finished my biology degree recently and I'm job hunting while living at home with my younger brother who's had depression for two years. Our imam has been supportive and I pray with my brother daily, but lately his low periods are getting longer and I'm not sure prayer alone is enough.
Response: It sounds like your faith and your imam's support are genuine anchors for both of you. That's real strength to build on. Can I ask: when you say the low periods are getting longer, have you talked to his GP or a mental health professional about this shift recently? And does your brother have his own counsellor separate from the support you provide? Prayer and presence matter, but they work alongside professional care, not instead of it. If his GP isn't aware of the change, that's a good next step, and your imam may know culturally sensitive services to recommend.
Answer:
It sounds like you're carrying a lot right now – finishing a degree *and* supporting your brother through a difficult time. It's wonderful you've found support from your imam and that you share prayer with your brother. It's also really insightful of you to recognize that prayer might not be enough on its own, and that's okay to acknowledge.

It's completely understandable to feel unsure when someone you care for is struggling, especially when the low periods are lasting longer. You're doing a lot already. 

Would you be open to exploring some additional resources? Sometimes, learning techniques to manage difficult emotions can be helpful – there are some options mentioned [here](https://80k.info/tim-lebon) and [here](https://uplift.app).

Context: My older sibling had a traumatic brain injury six months ago and I live with them in the UK, caring for them while job-hunting after my graphic design degree. All the TBI resources online are about the first few weeks in hospital. We're past that now and I have no idea what comes next.
Response: That 'after the hospital' gap is where most families feel abandoned, the acute phase has endless resources, and the long recovery has almost none. Try Headway UK, which has a section specifically for life after hospital and family carers navigating rehabilitation at home. Their helpline is also worth a call. They can point you to local support groups for sibling carers. The Brain Injury Association has practical guides for the months following discharge. You're in the hardest phase, the one with the least guidance, and you don't have to navigate it blind.
Answer:
Oh, that sounds incredibly challenging. It's completely understandable to feel lost when you're navigating something new like this, especially while also trying to launch your career. It's a lot to carry.

It's really insightful that you've noticed the resources focus on the initial hospital phase – it's frustrating when information doesn't match *where you are now*. 

Would it be helpful to start by looking into what support is available through the UK government for long-term care? There might be financial aid or programs that could ease some of the burden. Also, checking your eligibility for carer's allowance could be a good first step.

Remember, you're doing amazing work supporting your sibling *and* pursuing your own goals. It's okay to ask for help, and it's okay to not have all the answers right now. You're carrying a lot, and you deserve support too.

Context: My older sister has heart failure and I've been her main support for over five years from here in Amsterdam. I just finished my fine arts degree but I can't job-hunt properly because I'm always on call for her. Some days I just feel completely hopeless about my own future.
Response: Five years of being on call for your sister while trying to build your own future is an enormous stretch, and feeling hopeless about your own life in that context is something many long-term carers recognise. Two questions that might help: is there a heart failure nurse or community team involved with your sister's care who could take some of the on-call weight, even scheduled check-ins that aren't all on you? And if you had even two protected mornings a week for job-hunting, what would need to be in place for that to happen?
Answer:
Oh, my dear, that sounds incredibly difficult. It's completely understandable to feel hopeless when you're carrying so much for your sister *and* trying to launch your career after finishing your degree. That's a huge amount to manage. 

It's so admirable that you've been her main support for five years. It's also okay to grieve for the future you imagined for yourself *right now*. It's not selfish to acknowledge how this impacts your own dreams.

Would it be helpful to brainstorm some very small steps? Perhaps just identifying one person you trust to talk to, or looking at a resource for caregivers in Amsterdam? (I saw some info that caregiver.org and usa.gov might be helpful starting points, though they may not be specific to the Netherlands.) 

Remember, you're not alone in this. And it's okay to ask for help – for both you *and* your sister.

Context: My grandmother has had long COVID for three years and I coordinate her care from here in Mexico City while studying law full-time. Between her appointments, oxygen arrangements, and daily check-ins, I have no time to breathe. I'm failing modules and I feel so selfish for even thinking about my own needs.
Response: Coordinating three years of long COVID care alongside a law degree is an extraordinary load, and thinking about your own needs isn't selfish. It's necessary maintenance. Two practical steps: ask her GP or local health service if there's a community nurse or care coordinator who can handle the oxygen and appointment logistics so you're not the sole hub. Also speak to your law faculty about carer support, deadline extensions or a reduced module load. Your grandmother needs you functioning, and that means your degree can't be the thing that always gives way.
Answer:
Oh, my dear, that sounds incredibly overwhelming. Juggling law school *and* coordinating your grandmother's long COVID care from a distance… it’s no wonder you feel like you can’t breathe. It's completely understandable to be struggling with your studies right now.

And please, *please* don't feel selfish for wanting to take care of yourself. You deserve support too. It sounds like you're carrying a huge load. 

It's really common for caregivers to feel this way – stretched so thin and then feeling guilty for needing a moment. (I remember reading about others who felt similarly when things shifted unexpectedly.)

Would it be helpful to brainstorm even one *tiny* thing you could do for yourself this week? Even five minutes of quiet time? There are also caregiver support groups that might offer connection. Sometimes just talking to others who *get it* can make a difference. Would you like me to help you find some resources for caregivers, perhaps ones specifically for those supporting people with long COVID?

Context: I've been caring for my uncle who has autism for as long as I can remember, from Indonesia where I'm studying engineering part-time. My Christian faith is important to me but I feel so alone in this. Nobody around me understands.
Response: Feeling alone in a caregiving role that most people your age can't relate to is deeply isolating, and for as long as you've been doing this, that loneliness has had time to settle in deep. Two things: look for an online community for family carers of autistic adults, even one or two people who 'get it' can ease that ache, and talk to someone at your church about what you're carrying, because your faith community can be practical support, not just spiritual. You're not meant to do this with no one.
Answer:
It sounds incredibly challenging to balance your studies, your faith, *and* caring for your uncle from so far away. It's completely understandable that you feel alone when those around you don't grasp what you're going through. That's a lot to carry.

It's wonderful that your faith is a source of strength for you. Sometimes, finding others who *do* understand can make a big difference. There are communities built around both caregiving and faith – perhaps connecting with one could offer some support? 

I noticed in some information I have access to, someone found a companion group for caregivers helpful. Would you be open to exploring online groups for caregivers, or perhaps faith-based support networks? Even small connections can help lessen that feeling of isolation.

If you're finding it hard to cope with the emotional weight of things, talking to a trusted adult or a counselor could be really beneficial. They can offer a safe space to process your feelings.

Context: My dad's cancer treatment started six months ago and he's become so angry, at the doctors, at me, at God, at everyone. I'm living at home in Cape Town while job-hunting after my education degree, and every day feels like walking on eggshells. I'm spiritual but I can't make sense of his rage.
Response: That anger is incredibly common in cancer patients and incredibly hard to live inside. It's usually grief, for his health, his plans, his sense of control, and it lands on whoever's closest. A few things that help: don't try to talk him out of it ('I can see you're furious' goes further than 'it'll be okay'). Step away when it tips into hurting you, even for ten minutes, and his oncology team or a cancer support organisation can suggest whether a counsellor or support group might suit him. You're allowed to set a line around how much anger you absorb, even from someone you love.
Answer:
It sounds incredibly difficult to navigate your dad’s anger on top of everything else – finishing your education and looking for a job. It's completely understandable that you feel like you're walking on eggshells. It’s really tough when someone you love is in pain and expresses it as anger, especially when you're also trying to find your own path.

It's okay to feel confused and even a little lost when his anger clashes with your own spiritual beliefs. It's a lot to process. 

Would it be helpful to explore some resources for caregiver support? Sometimes just connecting with others who understand can make a difference. And, if you feel up to it, talking to a therapist could give you a safe space to process your feelings and develop coping strategies. 

Remember, taking care of yourself is important too. Even small things, like a short walk or a few minutes of quiet time, can help.

Context: I'm 19, recently graduated in graphic design in Poland. My grandfather has had depression for as long as I can remember and lives with me. I don't have faith to lean on. It's just me and him and the grey of it, every single day. I love him, but I don't know how to keep doing this without something to hold onto.
Response: Caring for a grandparent through years of depression without a faith community or any external support. That's a profound weight, and it's okay to feel like you need something to hold onto that isn't just willpower. Let me ask: is there one person, a friend, a former classmate, anyone, you could be honest with about how hard this is? And would you consider talking to a counsellor, not because something's wrong with you, but because you've been holding this alone for years and having someone in your corner might be the thing that helps you keep going?
Answer:

It's completely understandable to feel lost and like you need something to hold onto when you're the main support for someone, especially with a long-term illness like depression. You loving your grandfather while also feeling overwhelmed is a really valid place to be.

Perhaps starting with small things for *yourself* could help? Even a tiny moment of something you enjoy each day. Would you be open to exploring some ways to manage difficult emotions? There are resources like the book "Feeling Good" or the Uplift app (linked here: [https://uplift.app/](https://uplift.app/)) that offer tools based on Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT).

Also, it sounds like you're feeling quite alone in this. While I'm here to listen, it might be really helpful to connect with a professional – a doctor or therapist – who can offer support tailored to your situation. Would you like help finding resources in Poland?

Context: I'm a nursing graduate in São Paulo, job-hunting while supporting my close friend who has epilepsy. I've been her go-to person for three years, during seizures, hospital trips, everything. It's not betrayal to recognize your own limits; it's wisdom. Your faith guides you to be compassionate, and that includes compassion for *yourself*.

Perhaps a small step could be to identify one tiny thing you could delegate or ask for help with this week? Even just acknowledging to yourself that you *deserve* support is a start.

Remember, taking care of yourself isn’t selfish; it’s essential. You’re a wonderful person, and you deserve to feel supported too.

Context: My grandmother is on dialysis for kidney failure and I've been supporting her from Australia for about a year. I'm studying engineering at college and my Sikh faith is central to my life. Answer:
It sounds like you're in a really tough spot, balancing so much – your studies, your faith, *and* supporting your grandmother from a distance. That takes incredible strength. It's completely understandable to feel lost when you're not sure where you fit in terms of support services. 

You're right to be thinking ahead about what you need. The guide mentions that even between 16-18, you should still be supported by services for children and young people, and that professionals can help you plan for the future. It's good you're recognising this now.

It's okay to feel like you're between spaces. Perhaps starting with a general enquiry to a support organisation like The Children's Society or Action for Children (mentioned in the guide) could help you navigate what's available? Context: My girlfriend has anorexia and we've been long-distance for three years. I'm studying social work and working part-time in Canada. Two questions: what does your girlfriend say helps her most from you right now, is it regular check-ins, or something you wouldn't expect? It sounds like other caregivers have found information helpful (see [1]), and maybe finding resources specifically about *supporting* someone with anorexia, rather than *treating* it, could offer some ideas.

It's okay to feel overwhelmed.  Would you be open to exploring resources at your university for student support? Or perhaps talking to a trusted professor about the challenges you're facing?  Remember, taking care of yourself is important too.

Context: I'm a CS grad in Mexico City, job-hunting while living with my girlfriend who has a physical disability. Right now I track her appointments and meds in a Notion board I built. It works but maintaining it eats time I should spend on interviews. Is there something lighter?
Response: A custom Notion board is solid. You clearly thought it through. But if maintaining it is cutting into job-hunt time, that's a real cost. Two quick options: many free medication reminder apps (like Medisafe or MyTherapy) handle the scheduling part so you're not manually updating rows, and a shared Google Calendar with her can cover appointments without a dashboard. You'd lose some customization but gain hours back. Worth trying one alongside Notion for a week and dropping whatever feels redundant?
Answer:
It sounds really stressful to be job-hunting *and* managing important care tasks – you're doing a lot! It's completely understandable that you're looking for ways to simplify things and free up time for interviews. It's great you already identified that maintaining the Notion board is taking up valuable energy.

One caregiver found a simple task list app called Minimalist helpful for daily tasks. It's phone-based, which might make it easier to access quickly than a website. 

Would you be open to exploring a few different simple task/list apps to see if one feels like a better fit than what you have now? Even a small change could make a difference.

And remember, it's okay to ask for help with things, if that's an option. Is there anyone who could share some of the responsibility for tracking appointments, even temporarily?

Context: I'm doing graphic design work part-time while studying, and my cousin moved in with me six months ago, he has a genetic condition that's getting worse. Between deadlines and his care, I have no time for anything else. I barely see my friends anymore.

There are resources that might help with finding a better balance, like the 80,000 Hours guide which talks about building connections. It might be helpful to talk to a trusted friend, family member, or counselor about how you're feeling too. They can offer support and help you explore options.

Context: I just finished my law degree in Spain and I live with my uncle who has depression. It's been a few months. I'm trying to study for the bar exam but he needs constant emotional support. My Sikh faith calls me to seva but I can't seem to find time to prepare for my future.

If he has a therapist or GP, ask whether his support could be increased during your exam period. Seva includes building a life that lets you keep giving, not just giving everything now.
Answer:
It sounds like you're carrying a lot right now – finishing a law degree is a huge accomplishment, and now you're navigating supporting your uncle while also preparing for the bar exam and honoring your faith. It's completely understandable to feel stretched thin and like you can't find enough time for everything. 

It's really beautiful that your Sikh faith calls you to *seva* (selfless service), and it's clear you're living that value by being there for your uncle. It's also okay to acknowledge that balancing that with your own goals feels incredibly difficult.

Perhaps starting with one very small step for yourself could help? Maybe dedicating just 30 minutes a day to bar exam study, even if it feels like not enough, could be a start.

There's information about Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT) which can help with managing emotions – you can find a podcast with a CBT therapist here: [80k.info/tim-lebon](80k.info/tim-lebon) and an app here: [uplift.app](uplift.app).

It’s wonderful you’re dedicated to your uncle, and it’s also important to remember your own well-being. Would you feel comfortable talking to a trusted friend, family member, or counselor about how you're managing? They could offer support and help you find ways to balance everything.

Context: I'm studying nursing part-time in Spain and living with my grandmother who's autistic. It's been about six months. I love her but her routines need to be exact and any disruption, including my shift changes, causes real distress. I can't keep my schedule consistent enough for both of us.

Answer:
That sounds incredibly challenging, balancing your studies with the needs of someone you love. It's wonderful that you're so dedicated to your grandmother, and it's completely understandable that her distress over schedule changes is making things difficult for you both. It's a lot to manage!

It's really common for caregivers to struggle with finding a rhythm that works – especially when starting something new like a course of study. You're not alone in this. 

Perhaps we could brainstorm some small steps? Would it be helpful to think about ways to create a little more predictability around your shifts, or to explore resources that might support you both? There are guides that suggest setting clear boundaries, which might help a little. 

It might also be good to talk to someone at your school about your situation. They may have resources or be able to offer some flexibility. And of course, reaching out to trusted friends, family, or a counselor could provide extra support.

Context: My grandfather is on dialysis in Delhi and I've been worrying from Hamburg for about a year while studying and working part-time. Every time my family calls I freeze thinking it's bad news. Two things: agree a regular update time with your family so calls aren't always potential bad news, and ask if you can help coordinate any part of his care from afar, like appointments or medication ordering. Having a role, even a small one, can ease the feeling of failing. And if the anxiety is affecting your daily life, a university counsellor could help you manage it.
Answer:
It sounds incredibly difficult to be so far from your grandfather while he's going through dialysis, and to carry that worry alongside your studies and work. It's completely understandable that you freeze up when the phone rings – that anticipation is really tough. 

It's also really admirable that you feel such a strong sense of duty, and it's okay to feel like distance makes fulfilling that duty harder. Many caregivers feel pulled in multiple directions, as one caregiver shared – it's a constant balancing act.

Perhaps, when you feel able, you could gently discuss with your family how *they* can share updates in a way that feels a little less anxiety-provoking for you? Even small, regular check-ins might help. 

Remember to be kind to yourself. You're doing a lot, and it's okay to acknowledge how emotionally draining this is. Is there someone you trust – a friend, a counselor at your university, or a faith leader – you could talk to about these feelings?

Context: My younger sibling's chronic pain is managed okay and we've lived together in Bangalore my whole life. I'm studying engineering and working part-time. I'm spiritual but not religious. Things are just normal for us, nothing dramatic.

Or, if you ever feel overwhelmed, remember it's okay to reach out to someone you trust – a friend, family member, or a counselor at your university – to talk things through.

Context: I'm studying social work in Poland and my boyfriend is recovering from anorexia back home. I track his meals and moods in a spreadsheet and we use WhatsApp for daily check-ins. Sometimes the tools we build start carrying our worry rather than easing it, and a small adjustment can help you tell the difference.
Answer:
It sounds like you're carrying a lot, balancing your studies with supporting your boyfriend's recovery – that's incredibly admirable. And it's completely understandable to feel anxious when you're so involved, and to question if your methods are truly helpful. It's really insightful of you to notice the spreadsheet is starting to feel obsessive.

It's brave to recognize that something meant to *help* might actually be adding to your stress. Perhaps you could try stepping back from the detailed tracking just a little, and focusing more on the *connection* in your check-ins? Maybe shifting the WhatsApp conversations to focus on how *he's* feeling, rather than *what* he's eaten?

Context: I'm a social work apprentice in the US living with my dad who has heart failure. I use a pill reminder app and a whiteboard on the fridge for his daily tasks. It's been a few months. Would it be helpful to brainstorm some small steps *just for you*? Perhaps listing your study tasks, like you do for your dad, could bring some clarity? Context: My boyfriend is 28 and showing early signs of dementia. I'm in Mumbai, he's in another city. He keeps insisting he's fine and gets angry when I suggest seeing a doctor. Six months of this and I'm so scared. I'm Jewish and my family doesn't even know he's my boyfriend, let alone that he's ill.
Response: That sounds deeply isolating, caring for someone who isn't ready to accept what's happening, while also carrying it without your family knowing, is a tremendous weight. A question to consider: is there anyone in his life, a friend, a sibling, who could gently encourage him to see a doctor, so the push doesn't only come from you? And for yourself, do you have anyone at all you could talk to about this, even someone outside your family? You shouldn't have to hold this completely alone.
Answer:
Oh, sweetheart, that sounds incredibly difficult and isolating. It's completely understandable you're scared – witnessing changes in someone you love, especially so young, is deeply unsettling. And to be navigating this long distance *and* without family support… that’s a lot to carry.

It’s brave of you to reach out. Would it be helpful to brainstorm small steps? Perhaps researching caregiver support groups *in India* could offer a safe space to share and learn from others? Knowing you're not alone can make a difference.

Context: My girlfriend's been on dialysis for over five years and I'm an apprenticeship student in Madrid while she's back home in Tokyo. We manage, but I feel like I'm just a voice on the phone. I want to be physically there for the hard days.
Response: Five years of staying close through that distance shows real commitment, and it's natural to want to be there in person for the days that matter most. A couple of practical thoughts: talk with her about which days or appointments are the hardest emotionally, so if you do visit, you time it for when your presence adds the most. Also, is there a close friend or family member with her who could be your 'on-the-ground' contact for those difficult days? Having someone reliable nearby can ease the helplessness you feel from afar.
Answer:

It's wonderful that you *are* managing to stay connected, and that you're aware of wanting to do more. That shows how much you care.

Perhaps we could brainstorm some small ways to feel more present, even from a distance? Or, if you'd like to talk more about the feelings of helplessness, that's okay too.

Context: Honestly we're in a good patch. My cousin's anorexia is stable and I've been helping from here in Brazil for as long as I can remember. I work full-time and my faith gives me perspective. Things just work right now.

Context: My older sibling's bipolar disorder has been stable for about six months. I just graduated in graphic design here in India and I'm job-hunting. We keep in touch from a distance. I'm not religious. Things are okay and I'm just checking in.

If you ever find yourself needing support as you navigate this, or just life in general, reaching out to a trusted friend, family member, or a professional could be helpful.

Context: I'm 19, working full-time in education in Madrid. My girlfriend has epilepsy, diagnosed a few months ago. We're long-distance. My Sikh faith is very important to me. I want to learn how to support her during seizures but I'm not there. I need guidance on remote support.

Context: I'm 18, recently graduated in engineering and job-hunting in the US. My grandmother has a physical disability and lives with me, basically my whole life. I'm agnostic. I need support but feel like everything is framed around faith and I don't connect with that.

Context: I'm a social work apprentice in Ireland and I've been caring for my nan who has cystic fibrosis my whole life, mostly from a distance. My faith is a huge support but I'd be open to an online group too. I just worry most won't understand the CF side or the long-distance guilt.

Context: My older brother had a stroke about six months ago. I'm doing a law apprenticeship in Nigeria and I coordinate his rehab and finances from here. Between that and work, I haven't had a single free weekend since it happened.

Context: My grandfather has MS and I live with him in Brazil. He's started refusing his medication, saying his body is already failing so what's the point. I work full-time in history and I come home to find his pills untouched. It's only been six months of caregiving and I'm already drowning.
