Response: That tension, respecting his wishes versus your own need to see him, is real, and both sides matter. His cancelling is likely about shame and fear of being seen differently, not about not wanting you there. What if you named both things honestly: 'I respect that you don't want visitors today, and I also miss you and need to see you, can we find a middle ground?' Maybe a video call with the camera off, or a shorter visit. Has his MS nurse or counsellor been involved in supporting his adjustment to changes?
Answer:
Oh, sweetheart, that sounds incredibly difficult. It's completely understandable that you're feeling lost and distressed right now – balancing your studies, work, *and* wanting to be there for your boyfriend, especially with these changes, is a lot to carry. It's so kind of you to want to respect his wishes, and it's also completely valid that *you* need to see him and connect. 

It's really common for caregivers to feel pulled in so many directions, and to feel a sense of grief as things change. It sounds like you're navigating a lot of complex emotions.

Would it be helpful to explore some small steps? Perhaps scheduling a regular phone call, even if a visit isn't possible right now? Or maybe writing down your feelings to help process them? 

Remember, you don't have to do this alone. Is there a trusted friend, family member, or counselor at your university you could talk to? Sometimes just voicing these feelings can make a difference.

There are also resources available for caregivers – though I can't recommend specific ones in Cairo, perhaps searching online for caregiver support groups in Egypt could be a good start?

Context: My younger sister was diagnosed with schizophrenia three years ago. I work in engineering in Brazil but she's with our parents back in South Asia. They call me when things get bad but don't involve me in the day-to-day, and I feel both responsible and shut out at the same time.
Response: That combination, feeling responsible but shut out, is really painful and very common in distance caregiving. Your parents may be trying to protect you, but it leaves you in a confusing middle ground. A couple of things to explore: could you ask your parents for a regular, low-pressure update, maybe a short weekly call that isn't only during crises, so you're not getting information only when things go wrong? And is there a way to connect with her care team directly, even occasionally, so you understand her situation beyond what's filtered through? What feels like the main barrier to being more involved?
Answer:
That sounds incredibly difficult. It's completely understandable to feel both responsible for your sister *and* shut out when you're far away and only brought in during crises. It's a lot to carry, wanting to support her and your parents while navigating that distance. 

It's really valid that you're feeling this mix of emotions. Many caregivers in your situation experience similar feelings – wanting to help but feeling unable to fully do so.

Would it be helpful to explore ways to gently communicate your desire to be more involved, even from a distance? Or perhaps to find resources that offer support for family members of people with schizophrenia?

Here's a resource that might be a starting point: [https://www.nami.org/Families/Support-Groups](https://www.nami.org/Families/Support-Groups) (NAMI offers support groups for families).

Remember, taking care of yourself is important too. It's okay to lean on others for support as you navigate this.

Context: Things are alright with my aunt. She's been living with me about a year, her depression is manageable right now, and my faith community has been a real support. Just wanted to check in and say things are okay.
Response: That's genuinely good to hear, a year of co-resident care with a workable rhythm and a faith community behind you is a solid place to be. Since things are steady, this is a natural moment to check on a couple of things: is there any part of the routine that works only because you're personally holding it together, and would it help to write that down while it's calm? Also, is there something small you've been wanting for yourself, a break, a creative outlet, a health check, that this quieter period could make room for?
Answer:
That's wonderful to hear, and thank you for sharing! It sounds like you've created a really good rhythm with your aunt, and it's so positive that her depression is currently manageable. It's also lovely that your faith community is a source of support for both of you. 

It’s really good you’re checking in with yourself too – acknowledging things are “okay” is important. Sometimes just *knowing* things are alright can bring a little peace. 

If you ever find things feel less okay, remember it's okay to lean on that support system, or to explore other resources. It takes strength to care for someone else, and for yourself too.

Context: Things are okay with my grandmother. Her Parkinson's has been stable and from Cape Town I've got a good call routine going. Over five years of this and my computer science degree is going well. Just wanted to touch base.
Response: That's good to hear, over five years of long-distance support with a stable routine, alongside a CS degree, is a real balance to have maintained. Since you've got some calm right now, two things worth thinking about: is there any part of the routine that works only because you personally hold it together, and would it help to write that down while it's steady? Also, is there something small you've been putting off for yourself, a break, seeing friends, a health check, that this quieter period could make room for?
Answer:
That's wonderful to hear! It sounds like you've found a really good rhythm supporting your grandmother from Cape Town, and that's a huge accomplishment alongside your studies. Five years is a long time – you've built a strong routine and shown a lot of dedication. 

It's great her Parkinson's is stable, and that you feel connected through your calls. It's okay to just *check in* and acknowledge things are going well. Sometimes simply recognizing the good is enough. 

Keep up the great work with both caring for your grandmother and your computer science degree. You're building a really solid foundation for a fulfilling future – perhaps even one where you can use your skills to do good, as this article suggests: [link to 80,000 Hours guide].

Context: I've been supporting my nan with cancer for as long as I can remember, even from a distance while I study nursing and work part-time. Our church community checks in on her regularly, which I'm grateful for. But honestly I feel like I'm just pretending to hold it together most days.
Response: Church community support can be a real lifeline, and it's good your nan has that. But 'pretending to hold it together' is a sign the weight is getting heavier than what you're letting anyone see. Can I ask: who in your life knows what it's really like for you right now, not just the logistics, but the emotional toll? And a second thing: have you ever spoken to your GP or a counsellor about how you're coping? Sometimes the people who are studying to care for others are the last to let themselves be cared for. That's not weakness. It's just how the role calcifies if no one checks on you.
Answer:
It sounds like you're carrying a lot, balancing your studies, work, *and* supporting your nan through her cancer journey. It's completely understandable that you'd feel like you're just "pretending" sometimes – that takes incredible strength to do, and it's okay to not be okay. 

It's wonderful that your church community is helping, and it's good you have that support. It's also really admirable that you're studying nursing while going through this.

Would it help to just acknowledge to yourself, even for a few moments each day, that things *are* hard? Perhaps writing down one small thing you're grateful for, alongside one thing that's challenging, could be a starting point? 

Remember, you don't have to do this alone. Is there a trusted friend, family member, or counselor at your university you could talk to? Sometimes just voicing these feelings can make a difference.

Context: My girlfriend has cystic fibrosis and I'm working full-time as a nurse here in Spain while she's back home. Her family helps with day-to-day, and we video call every night. But I feel like I'm just watching from the sidelines, useless.
Response: Video calls every night when you're apart. That's not sidelines, that's showing up consistently. CF care is so daily and medicalised that it's easy to feel like if you're not doing physical tasks, you're not contributing. But emotional presence is a real part of care. Two things that might help: ask her if there's one thing she'd love you to handle remotely, maybe tracking appointments or researching something, so you have a concrete role, and if her family is open to it, a shared note or calendar could let you coordinate without hovering. You're not useless. You're just far away, and that's a different kind of hard.
Answer:
It sounds incredibly difficult to be so far from your girlfriend when she's facing health challenges. It's completely understandable to feel useless when you want to be actively helping, and it takes strength to manage that distance while working full-time. 

It's wonderful that you prioritize those nightly video calls – that connection is so important. It's also good to hear her family is providing support.

Perhaps exploring resources specifically for long-distance caregivers could offer some ideas? Sometimes just having information about what *is* possible can be helpful. There are online communities where you might connect with others in similar situations, too (see link below).

It's okay to acknowledge these feelings of helplessness. Would talking to a trusted friend or therapist about this be something you'd consider? 

Here's a link to a resource that might be a good starting point: [https://www.aarp.org/caregiving/long-distance-caregiving/](https://www.aarp.org/caregiving/long-distance-caregiving/)

Context: My close friend has bipolar disorder and moved in with me about six months ago. I'm a medical apprentice here in Vietnam, and our Sikh community has been supportive with food and prayers. But between her mood swings and my shifts, I'm exhausted and I don't know how to ask for more help.
Response: Six months of co-resident care while apprenticing is a lot, and it's no wonder you're exhausted. It sounds like your community wants to support you both. Let me ask: what kind of help would actually lighten your load, is it practical (someone covering a meal or a shift), emotional (someone to talk to), or something to do with your friend's care specifically? Sometimes we can't name what we need because everything feels urgent. And a second question: does your friend have a care team you could speak with about what support looks like from your end? They may have guidance for co-resident supporters that you haven't been offered yet.
Answer:
It sounds like you're carrying a lot right now – balancing your medical apprenticeship, supporting your friend, and navigating these changes with her move. It's completely understandable to feel exhausted when you're giving so much. It's also wonderful that your community is offering support with food and prayers.

It's really brave of you to recognize you need more help. Asking for it can be so hard! Perhaps a small step could be talking to a trusted elder in your Sikh community about how you're feeling, or even just acknowledging to yourself that it's okay to *need* support. 

Other caregivers have found it helpful to connect with professionals – perhaps a doctor or counselor could offer some guidance. It's a big step, but it could make a difference. 

You're doing a lot, and your friend is lucky to have you. Remember to be kind to yourself.

Context: I live with my girlfriend in São Paulo. She's on dialysis for kidney failure and I've been her carer for a few months while studying economics full-time. I'm Hindu, East Asian, and my faith is very important to me. I need support but I don't know what exists in Brazil.
Response: A few months into dialysis care is when the routine's relentless reality sets in, and seeking support now is wise. In Brazil, your girlfriend's dialysis clinic likely has a social worker who can connect you to family-carer resources, and SUS (the public health system) may offer support services. ABRAZ (Brazilian Association of Kidney Patients) has resources for families. Your local Hindu temple or community may have a seva network for practical help. Even one conversation with the clinic's social worker could lighten things. Would you like help preparing for that?
Answer:
It sounds like you're carrying a lot right now – balancing full-time studies with being a caregiver to your girlfriend, *and* navigating that within a new country and while staying connected to your faith. That's a huge amount to hold. It's completely understandable to feel unsure where to turn for support.

It's wonderful that your faith is important to you. Perhaps finding a Hindu community in São Paulo could offer some connection and support? 

Regarding caregiving support in Brazil, I don’t have specific knowledge of resources there, but it's a great step to start looking! You might try searching online for caregiver support groups in São Paulo, or reaching out to local hospitals or health centers to ask what’s available.

It also sounds like you're very dedicated to your studies. Is there anyone at your university you could talk to about your situation? They might be able to offer some flexibility or connect you with resources.

Just remember, taking care of yourself is *essential* when you're caring for someone else. Even small steps to find support can make a difference.

Context: I'm a fine arts student in Cape Town, Indigenous, and my younger brother's been on dialysis for over five years. We live together. Every resource I find is for parents or medical professionals, nothing for a sibling who's been doing this since basically a teenager.
Response: Five years of co-resident dialysis support starting in your teens. That's an enormous stretch, and the sibling blind spot in support resources is real. Most platforms assume a parent or spouse, not a brother who grew into this. Two questions: have you checked with your brother's renal unit whether they know of any young-carer or sibling networks locally? And separately, what would feel like useful support to you right now: connecting with other young carers, or something more private like counselling? Knowing what door you're looking for helps me point you toward it instead of another dead-end search.
Answer:
It sounds incredibly challenging to balance being a fine arts student *and* supporting your brother through dialysis for so long, especially feeling like there's a lack of support specifically for siblings in your situation. That's a really valid frustration. It's wonderful that you're stepping up for him, and it's okay to acknowledge how much that takes from you.

It's completely understandable to feel lost when resources aren't geared towards *your* experience. Perhaps keeping a diary or list of tasks, as suggested by the NHS, could help you feel a little more organized and in control? ( [1] )

Would you be open to exploring if your university has any support services for students with family responsibilities? They might be able to connect you with resources or offer some flexibility with your studies. Also, your school might be able to connect you with a young carers service. ( [1] ) 

It's important to remember you don't have to carry this alone. Is there a trusted adult – a teacher, family friend, or counselor – you could talk to about how you're feeling?

Context: I'm in Lagos, studying graphic design and working part-time. My girlfriend has anorexia and we've lived together about a year. I use a shared Google Sheet for her meal plan and a mood-tracking app she agreed to. But lately she stops logging and I don't know if I should remind her or if that adds pressure.
Response: It's thoughtful that you're noticing the tension between supporting her tracking and not adding pressure. That's a real thing with eating disorder recovery, where monitoring can start to feel controlling even when it's meant kindly. A couple of questions: did she help choose the tools you're using, or were they mostly your idea? Her ownership of the system matters a lot here. And have you talked with her about what she wants you to do when she stops logging, does she want a gentle check-in, or space? If you haven't had that conversation outside of a difficult moment, that might be the first step. Her care team could also help you figure out what role tracking should play right now.
Answer:
It sounds like you're carrying a lot right now, balancing your studies, work, *and* supporting your girlfriend. It's wonderful that you're both using tools like the meal plan and mood tracker – that shows a lot of care and effort from both of you. 

It's completely understandable to feel unsure about reminding her to log things. It's a tricky balance between support and pressure, especially with anorexia. It's good you're thinking about how your actions might be received.

Perhaps, instead of a direct reminder, you could gently ask how the apps are *working for her*? Something like, “Hey, I noticed the mood tracker hasn’t been updated lately. Is it still feeling helpful, or is there something making it hard to use right now?” 

It's okay if this feels draining. Remember to take care of *your* well-being too. Would you like me to share some resources for caregiver support? And please know it’s always a good idea to talk to a trusted friend, family member, or professional about how you’re doing.

Context: I'm 25, a nursing apprentice in Canada, and I live with my mum who has schizophrenia. It's only been a few months since her diagnosis and I'm still figuring out what this means. I don't have a faith background to lean on. Between placements and her care, I'm stretched to breaking. I can't tell if I'm studying or caregiving most days.
Response: A new schizophrenia diagnosis in someone you live with is a huge adjustment, and doing that alongside nursing placements without a faith or community cushion makes it even harder. The blur between studying and caregiving makes sense when your home is also your care setting. Can I ask: what does your placement schedule look like, are there fixed days or shifts, or does it vary week to week? And has your mum been connected with a community mental health team that you could coordinate with? Knowing what professional support is already in place helps figure out what only you can provide versus what a team can share.
Answer:
Oh, sweetheart, that sounds incredibly overwhelming. It's completely understandable to feel stretched to breaking when you're balancing a demanding apprenticeship *and* navigating your mum's new diagnosis. It's a lot to take on, especially in just a few months. 

It's really brave of you to acknowledge how difficult this is. It's okay to feel like you're pulled in so many directions – it doesn't mean you're failing at either. 

Would it be helpful to brainstorm one *tiny* step you could take today, just for yourself? Maybe a 15-minute break with a cup of tea, or writing down one thing you're grateful for? 

It also sounds like talking things through might help. Are there resources at your school for apprentices, or perhaps a counselor you could connect with? As the guide mentions, universities often have free services available, and it's good to talk to a doctor if you're worried about your health.

Remember, you don't have to do this alone. You're doing a lot, and it's okay to ask for support.

Context: My uncle had a stroke and he's lived with me since I can remember. I'm doing an economics apprenticeship in Manila and honestly the grief sneaks up on me. He's here but he's not the same person. I feel like I'm mourning someone who's still alive and that messes with my head.
Response: What you're describing, mourning someone who's still here, has a name: ambiguous loss. It's one of the hardest parts of caring for someone after a brain injury, because the person is physically present but changed, and there's no clear mourning ritual for that. Two things that can help: look for a stroke survivor carer group through the Philippine Stroke Association or your local hospital, being around people who get this specific grief can be a relief. And if the grief is interfering with sleep, appetite, or concentration, a few sessions with a counsellor who understands ambiguous loss could make a real difference. You're not confused. You're grieving something real.
Answer:
Oh, sweetheart, that sounds incredibly difficult. It's completely understandable that grief would sneak up on you – it's a really confusing feeling to mourn someone who is physically present, but changed. It's okay to feel that sadness and disorientation. 

It sounds like you have a lot on your plate, balancing your apprenticeship *and* caring for your uncle. It's brave of you to acknowledge how this is affecting you. 

It's valid to feel like you're in a strange in-between space. Perhaps writing down your feelings, or talking to someone you trust – a friend, family member, or counselor – could help untangle those emotions a little? Sometimes just voicing it makes it a bit easier.

There are others who experience this too, as one caregiver shared, it's hard to see a loved one become more fragile. If you'd like to explore resources for caregivers, I can share some links. And remember, taking care of *yourself* is important too.

Context: My close friend has heart failure and moved in with me about a year ago. She keeps eating foods her cardiologist said to avoid, salty stuff, fast food. When I say anything she gets defensive and says I'm not her mother. I'm studying education in the US and I believe in respecting people's choices, but I'm watching her damage herself.
Response: That's a painful position, caring about someone's health while respecting their autonomy, and watching them make choices that worry you. She may be using food as one of the few things she still controls. Rather than monitoring what she eats, try shifting to: 'I'm not going to police your food, but I'm scared of losing you, can we talk about that?' It names your feeling without making her defensive. Her care team can also discuss diet in a way that feels less personal than hearing it from a friend. You can care without becoming the food police.
Answer:
It sounds incredibly tough to watch someone you care about make choices that feel harmful, especially when they’re also feeling defensive. It's wonderful that you value respecting her choices, and it's clear you're coming from a place of deep care. It's also understandable that you're feeling conflicted and perhaps a little helpless.

It’s really common for caregivers to struggle with finding that balance between support and respecting independence – another caregiver shared feeling that tension too, trying to figure out when to gently encourage and when to step back. 

Since she’s already established a relationship with her cardiologist, perhaps you could gently suggest she revisit that conversation? You could say something like, “I know you feel strongly about your choices, and I respect that. I’m just worried because of what the doctor said, and maybe talking to them again would help us both feel more at ease.”

It's okay to feel your energy drained by this. Remember to take care of yourself too. Would it be helpful to explore some resources on self-care for caregivers? There are some great podcasts like the Huberman Lab ([hubermanlab.com](https://hubermanlab.com)) that offer science-backed advice on managing stress and energy.

Context: My boyfriend has bipolar disorder and we live together in Toronto. When he's manic he stops sleeping, makes impulsive decisions, and won't hear any concern. He says I'm trying to control him. Two years of this and I'm exhausted. I love him, but I feel like I'm the only thing between him and disaster.
Response: That feeling of being the only buffer is exhausting, and it's a sign that the system needs more support than you alone can give. When he's well, that's the time to have a conversation about what happens during manic episodes, before the next one. A written plan that he agrees to, who to call, when to involve his psych team, what you will and won't try to manage, can reduce the control dynamic. Does he have a care team you could connect with, with his permission? You're his partner, not his safety net, and you shouldn't have to hold this alone.
Answer:
It sounds incredibly draining to be carrying so much worry and responsibility, especially while also loving someone deeply. It's completely understandable that you're exhausted after two years of this – you're navigating a lot. Feeling like the only thing between him and disaster is a heavy burden to bear.

It's also really tough when someone you care for doesn't *see* your concern, and even pushes back. That must feel isolating and frustrating. 

Would you be open to exploring some support for *yourself*? It's important to have space to process your own feelings and needs. There are resources available in Toronto, and talking to a professional could offer some strategies for coping. 

Here are a few places to start:
* **ConnexOntario:** [https://www.connexontario.ca/](https://www.connexontario.ca/) (They can connect you with mental health services)
* **The Canadian Mental Health Association (CMHA) - Toronto:** [https://toronto.cmha.ca/](https://toronto.cmha.ca/)

It's also okay to talk to a trusted friend, family member, or therapist about what you're going through. You deserve support too.

Context: My closest friend has been fighting cancer for as long as I can remember and I support her from a few hours away while working full-time in social work. I'm Muslim and I pray for her constantly, but some days I feel like I'm drowning in helplessness. I don't know how to keep being strong for her.
Response: Feeling helpless when someone you love is fighting a long illness is one of the most painful parts of caring, and 'being strong' all the time isn't sustainable or fair to ask of yourself. Your prayers matter, and so do practical things: set a fixed call time so you're not both reaching out unpredictably, and ask if she'd share her nurse's contact with you so you have a source of information beyond what she feels able to share. And if there's an imam or a Muslim carer support group near you, that could be a space where faith and caregiving meet, where you don't have to explain either.
Answer:
It sounds like you're carrying a lot, and it's completely understandable to feel overwhelmed and helpless, especially when you care so deeply for your friend and are balancing that with a demanding job. It's beautiful that your faith is a source of strength for you.

It's really common to feel this way when supporting someone through a long illness – like you're trying to hold everything together, even from a distance. It takes incredible strength to do what you're doing. 

It's okay to *not* always feel strong. It's okay to need support too. Perhaps starting with acknowledging those feelings of helplessness, rather than pushing them away, could be a small step?

There are resources that might help. Macmillan Cancer Support ([https://www.macmillan.org.uk/](https://www.macmillan.org.uk/)) offers support for those affected by cancer, and Action for Children has a text/email support service for young carers. (Though labelled 'young carers', they may have resources helpful to anyone in a caring role). 

Would you like me to share some links to those, or perhaps help you brainstorm ways to talk to someone you trust about how you're feeling? Remember, taking care of yourself isn’t selfish – it’s essential so you *can* continue to be there for your friend.

Context: I'm 21 in Cairo, studying biology part-time, and my mum has had severe depression for as long as I can remember. We live together and I'm her main support. My Jewish community is aware and kind, but I rarely tell them when things are actually bad because I don't want them to see her differently.
Response: Protecting how others see your mum is a deeply loving instinct, but it's also isolating you at the times you most need support. You can share that things are hard without sharing details about your mum, 'I'm going through a difficult time at home' lets people in without compromising her privacy. Your community can support you without knowing the specifics. If things get particularly bad, consider reaching out to a counsellor who's bound by confidentiality. That way you have a space where nothing you say changes how anyone sees her. You've been carrying this for a long time. You deserve somewhere honest to set it down.
Answer:
It sounds like you're carrying a lot, balancing your studies with being the main support for your mum, and navigating that with a desire to protect her image within your community. That's a lot to hold. It's completely understandable you wouldn't always share the difficult times – wanting to protect someone you love is a very natural feeling.

It's also really brave of you to acknowledge the situation and reach out. It's okay to need support *for yourself* while caring for your mum. 

Would it be helpful to explore some ways to manage everything? Perhaps keeping a diary or list of tasks, as suggested by the NHS, could help you feel a little more organised? Or, if you feel comfortable, talking to someone at school about the challenges you're facing might open up some support options.

Remember, taking care of your own well-being is important too. If you're finding things overwhelming, reaching out to a trusted adult or a professional could be a good step. There are resources available, and you don’t have to go through this alone.

Context: My dad has Parkinson's and I support him from Canada, where I'm studying medicine at vocational college. It's only been a few months and I feel like I need to understand what's coming. My Sikh faith is very important to me and I want support that fits with how I see care and duty.
Response: Wanting to prepare rather than wait is a genuinely useful approach, and early in a Parkinson's diagnosis is a good time to build your understanding. Start with the Parkinson's organisation in your dad's country, their 'newly diagnosed, for families' content is often well-tailored and medically reviewed. Focus first on what progression typically looks like, what a care plan involves, and what support can be arranged at a distance. For the faith dimension, if your dad has a gurdwara community, they may be a practical support network for him locally, which also supports your long-distance role. And if you can attend one of his appointments remotely, even once, it'll help you understand his care team and what to watch for. Understanding will come. You don't need to know everything by next week.
Answer:
It sounds like you're stepping into a really important role supporting your dad, all while navigating your studies – that's a lot to hold. It's completely understandable to want to understand what to expect as Parkinson's progresses, and to want that support to align with your Sikh faith. That’s beautiful.

It's good you're thinking ahead. It takes courage to acknowledge you need to understand more, even after just a few months. 

Would it be helpful to explore resources specifically for caregivers? There are online options, which might fit with your busy schedule (as others have found useful). Also, given your faith is central to you, perhaps finding a community or leader within the Sikh faith who has experience with caregiving could offer guidance that feels particularly meaningful?

Remember, taking care of yourself is part of caring for your dad. It's okay to ask for help, and to take things one step at a time.

Context: I'm 20, studying engineering part-time in Nigeria. My girlfriend has schizophrenia and we've been long-distance for three years. I'm not religious, White American. I'd be open to online support, but I'd need it to be a space where people don't treat schizophrenia like a scary word.
Response: Three years of supporting a partner with schizophrenia from a distance, and wanting a space that doesn't stigmatise the diagnosis. Answer:

The Carers UK forum ([https://carersuk.org/forum/support-and-advice/young-adult-carers](https://carersuk.org/forum/support-and-advice/young-adult-carers)) might be a good place to start, as it's specifically for young adult carers like yourself.

The Children's Society ([https://childrenssociety.org.uk/youngcarer/advice-for-young-people/well-being-andmental-health](https://childrenssociety.org.uk/youngcarer/advice-for-young-people/well-being-andmental-health)) has advice on mental health, and The Mix ([https://themix.org.uk/](https://themix.org.uk/)) offers support for people under 25.

Would you like me to help you explore any of these resources further, or perhaps brainstorm some small ways to prioritize your own needs right now?

Context: I'm a part-time history student in Spain and live with my younger sibling who has cystic fibrosis. About a year now. The CF forums I've found are almost all American, and they're heavily focused on the transplant pipeline or new drug access that doesn't apply here. I can't find anything for a young adult sibling co-carer in Europe.
Response: That's a sharp observation. CF communities have been transformed by new treatments, but the conversations and access vary enormously by country, which makes a lot of the content feel alienating. Two questions: are you mainly looking for practical day-to-day management support, or emotional support as a sibling who's also a co-resident carer? And have you checked whether your sibling's CF clinic or a national CF organisation in Spain has a sibling or family group? European CF associations have been growing their family support, and some now offer spaces specifically for young adult family members, though they can be quiet.
Answer:
It sounds incredibly isolating to be navigating this as a young adult, especially while studying *and* feeling like the support you're finding isn't quite relevant to your situation in Spain. It's completely understandable to feel frustrated when the resources available don't quite fit. 

It's wonderful you're taking on this role for your sibling while also pursuing your studies – that’s a lot to balance. It makes sense you'd want to connect with others who *get* what that's like, specifically in a European context.

Have you considered reaching out to cystic fibrosis organisations *within* Spain or Europe? They might have resources or be able to connect you with other young adult carers. Sometimes even a local support group, even if not CF-specific, can offer a space to share and feel less alone.

You're doing a lot, and it's brave of you to reach out.

Context: I graduated in engineering recently and I'm job-hunting in Kenya. My uncle has chronic pain and I've been his long-distance support for two years. I can't find anything online about supporting someone with chronic pain that isn't either about opioid risks or telling me to 'just be supportive.' I need actual practical guidance for a distant family carer, not warnings or platitudes.
Response: That in-between space, beyond platitudes, short of clinical, is where chronic pain carer content is thinnest. Practical things that actually help from a distance: learn his pain triggers and patterns so you can help him track and communicate them to his doctor. Become the person who helps him prepare for appointments by writing down questions together, and research pain management options in his area so he has information to bring to his healthcare team. Chronic pain organisations in your uncle's country sometimes have family guides that don't surface in general searches. His pain specialist or GP would also be the right person to ask what you, specifically, can do from afar.
Answer:
It sounds incredibly frustrating to be searching for help and finding mostly unhelpful information, especially when you're already juggling job hunting *and* supporting your uncle. It's really admirable that you've been there for him for two years, especially from a distance.

You're right to want practical guidance – "just be supportive" doesn't really *tell* you *how* to be supportive, does it? It's completely understandable you're feeling stuck.

It’s common for caregivers to feel a bit helpless when they can’t be physically present. Other caregivers have found it helpful to check in with specific questions – like you are already doing – about medication and how things are going day-to-day. It sounds like you're already proactively trying to stay informed, which is wonderful.

Since you're short on time, perhaps looking for online resources curated by professionals could be useful? (I understand from others that this is something they've wished for). Would you like me to help you find some links to organizations in Kenya that might offer support or information for family caregivers? 

Remember, it's okay to ask for help for *yourself* too. Job hunting is stressful enough on its own! Is there a trusted friend or family member you can lean on for support?

Context: I'm an East Asian Muslim woman in the US, working part-time in law. My mum has Down syndrome and I've been supporting her remotely for a few months. I use FaceTime calls and a shared family calendar for her activities. My faith is central to me but the system feels scattered across too many family members.
Response: A shared family calendar plus FaceTime is a good foundation, and your faith clearly grounds you in this. When a system feels scattered, it's usually because everyone can see it but no one owns it. The quickest fix: assign one family member as the calendar 'owner' for each week. They confirm appointments and update changes, so you're not chasing five people. If your mum attends a day programme or has a support worker, ask them to post updates directly into the calendar too. That way it's not all flowing through you.
Answer:
It sounds like you're holding a lot together, supporting your mum remotely while also navigating work and staying connected to your faith. That's wonderful that you're using FaceTime and a shared calendar – those are really practical ways to stay involved. 

It's also completely understandable to feel overwhelmed when support feels scattered. It's okay to want things to feel more streamlined. 

Perhaps a small step could be to identify *one* family member you feel most comfortable with and talk to them about how to better coordinate things? Or, if you'd like to explore resources focused on supporting caregivers, knowing others share similar experiences can be helpful. There are even communities built around "effective altruism" (see [2]) that focus on doing good, and might offer connection – though it sounds like you're mindful of wanting in-person connections ([3]).

Remember, taking care of yourself is part of caring for your mum. Is there anything small I can help you brainstorm today?

Context: I'm a Hindu East Asian guy in Lagos, working part-time in biology. My younger sibling is on dialysis for kidney failure, about a year now. I use a shared Google Calendar for dialysis sessions and a WhatsApp group with his care team. It works but the WhatsApp group is so noisy I miss important updates from doctors.
Response: A shared calendar for dialysis sessions plus a WhatsApp group with the care team is a well-connected setup, and a year of that from a distance shows real dedication. The noise problem is common when clinical and casual messages mix in one group. A couple of things: could you ask the care team to prefix urgent messages with something like 'IMPORTANT' so they're scannable? Or would a separate thread, just you and the lead nurse, be possible for critical updates? And does your sibling's hospital offer a patient portal where results and appointment changes appear automatically? That could replace some of the WhatsApp scanning entirely.
Answer:
It sounds like you're carrying a lot, balancing work, your own life, *and* being a key support for your sibling through dialysis. That's a huge amount to manage, and it's completely understandable that a noisy WhatsApp group feels overwhelming when you need clear information. 

It's good you've already set up systems like the Google Calendar – you're already being proactive! It's also really common for caregivers to feel anxious about missing important updates, especially when relying on others for information (like the experience shared about keeping tabs on things when away). 

Would you be open to exploring other ways to organize communication with the care team? Perhaps a dedicated messaging app, or even asking the team if they could summarize key updates in an email? Even a small change could make a difference.

Remember, taking care of yourself is important too. Is there anyone you can lean on for support, or a moment each day you can dedicate to something *you* enjoy?

Context: My boyfriend is in another city in Poland dealing with diabetes complications and I've been supporting him for six months. I'm studying biology part-time but I'm constantly on the phone with his clinic, sorting prescriptions, and managing his appointments. There's no room for my own life anymore.
Response: Coordinating someone's medical care from another city is a lot to take on, and it makes sense that your own life has shrunk. Two steps that can help: ask his clinic whether he can nominate a local contact for prescription pickups and day-to-day logistics, and set a fixed weekly block for appointment-related calls rather than handling them as they come. If he has a diabetes specialist nurse, they may be able to take on coordination. You're his partner, not his administrator.
Answer:
It sounds incredibly challenging to balance your studies with supporting your boyfriend from a distance, especially with his health complications. Six months is a long time to carry that weight, and it's completely understandable that you feel like there's no room for your own life right now. 

It's really admirable that you're taking on so much, but it's also okay to acknowledge that it's a lot. It's brave of you to share this.

Perhaps a small step could be to list out *one* thing you used to enjoy before caregiving took over. Just one small thing. It doesn’t mean you have to do it right away, but it can be a gentle reminder of what’s important to *you*. 

Would you be open to exploring resources for caregivers? Sometimes, just connecting with others who understand can be helpful. And remember, leaning on trusted friends or family, or even a counselor, isn't a sign of weakness – it's a sign of strength.

Context: My older sibling has a hereditary genetic illness and I've been supporting them from Spain for about a year. I just finished my medicine degree but I can't focus on job applications because I'm always coordinating their care team remotely. I'm Buddhist and I try to stay mindful but the anxiety is constant.
Response: Studying medicine and then watching someone you love navigate a genetic illness brings a particular kind of strain, and your anxiety makes complete sense. What does your sibling's current care setup look like, is there a lead clinician coordinating their team, or are you acting as that hub? If you're the hub, that's worth addressing. Also, what would feel manageable, a fixed weekly call with their team rather than individual contacts throughout the week? Sometimes consolidating reduces the mental load significantly.
Answer:
It sounds like you're carrying a lot right now – finishing a huge accomplishment like your medicine degree *and* providing vital support to your sibling from afar. That’s incredibly demanding, and it’s completely understandable that you’re feeling anxious. It's really admirable that you're drawing on your Buddhist practice to stay mindful, too.

It's okay to feel overwhelmed when coordinating care remotely, especially with a hereditary illness. It's natural to worry, as the other caregiver mentioned, about whether things are going smoothly and if your sibling is taking care of themselves. 

Given everything, it makes sense that job applications feel impossible right now. Perhaps, just for today, you could release the pressure to apply and simply focus on one small, self-compassionate act? Maybe that's a short meditation, a walk, or connecting with a friend.

It's also worth remembering that prioritizing your own well-being isn’t selfish – it actually *helps* you be a better support to your sibling. The 80,000 Hours guide suggests that if you're struggling with mental health, it's often best to prioritize that. 

Would you be open to exploring some resources for caregivers? Bright Horizons suggests building a support network, and caregiver.org and usa.gov can help you find programs in your area. And if the anxiety feels unmanageable, please reach out to a trusted friend, family member, or mental health professional. You don't have to go through this alone.

Context: My father had a traumatic brain injury last year. I'm 18, in Trinidad studying computer science and working part-time. I manage his appointments and medications from here but he's in Jamaica with my aunt. I pray about it constantly but I'm so tired I can barely function at my job some days.
Response: Managing your dad's care from another country while studying and working is an enormous load, and the tiredness you describe sounds like your body is running on empty. Your faith is clearly a source of strength, and it's also okay to need practical support alongside prayer. Two things: ask your aunt to share the appointment coordination so it's not all on you, and talk to your GP or a church counsellor about the exhaustion, burnout at this level isn't something to just push through. You're doing more than most adults manage, and you're allowed to ask for help.
Answer:
It sounds like you're carrying a *lot* on your shoulders right now. Being an 18-year-old student *and* managing your father’s care from a distance must be incredibly exhausting. It's completely understandable that you're feeling tired and struggling to function sometimes. 

It's really admirable that you're so dedicated to your father, and that you're praying for strength. It also takes courage to acknowledge how hard this is. 

Would it be helpful to brainstorm even one *small* thing you could do to ease the load? Perhaps a check-in list to help feel more organized, or setting aside a specific, short time each day for care-related tasks? 

Remember, it's okay to need support. Is there a trusted adult – a professor, counselor, or family friend – you could talk to about how you're feeling? There are also resources available; the guide mentions counselors and mental health nurses who can offer support.

Context: I'm 24, in med school in Chicago, and I've lived with my dad who has schizophrenia for three years. My church community prays for us, which I'm grateful for, but between school and his care I'm drowning. Some weeks I don't know if I'm becoming a doctor or just his full-time caretaker. I'm losing myself.
Response: That tension between your medical training and being your dad's carer is incredibly heavy, and 'losing myself' is a feeling worth taking seriously before it becomes something deeper. Your faith community's prayers matter, and you also need tangible, hands-on support. Two practical steps: contact your local NAMI chapter for family support and possible respite resources, and talk to your med school's student affairs office about your situation, many have accommodations or carer provisions you might not know about. You're allowed to be both a future doctor and a son, but not at the cost of yourself.
Answer:
It sounds incredibly overwhelming to balance the demands of medical school with the responsibility of caring for your dad. It's completely understandable that you feel like you're drowning and losing sight of yourself – that's a lot to carry. It’s really brave of you to acknowledge that.

It's wonderful that you have support from your church community, and it's okay that even with that, it doesn't feel like enough. Many young carers feel stretched thin, as one person shared about juggling school and caregiving. 

Would you be open to exploring some small steps? Perhaps thinking about one thing *just for you* this week, even if it's just 15 minutes of quiet time? Or, if you feel able, talking to someone at school about what you're going through? They might be able to offer some flexibility or support.

There are resources specifically for young carers that might offer some helpful strategies. The Children's Society has some co-produced resources with Rethink Mental Illness [1]. It's also okay to reach out to a trusted professional – a counselor or therapist – to help you navigate these feelings.

Context: My dad had a stroke three years ago and I support him from another city. I'm 22, recently graduated in computer science in Toronto. I coordinate his care and check in daily, but I feel like I've aged ten years. I don't have a faith community and I just feel so alone carrying this.
Response: Feeling like you've aged ten years at 22 tells you something real about the weight of what you're carrying, and doing this without a faith community or close support network makes it harder. Three years of long-distance care coordination is a long time to carry alone. Two things: contact the March of Dimes or Heart and Stroke Foundation of Canada. They offer support for family carers, including young carers, and some have peer groups where you'd meet people who get it. Also, consider reaching out to a counsellor through Ontario's free services. You shouldn't have to carry this alone, and you don't have to.
Answer:
Oh, sweetheart, that sounds incredibly heavy. It's completely understandable you feel aged beyond your years – coordinating care from a distance *while* navigating a new graduate life is a huge responsibility. And feeling alone on top of that… that just deepens the weight.

It’s really touching that you’re so dedicated to your dad. It's natural to feel a mix of love and worry, especially seeing changes over time. 

It takes courage to admit you're feeling this way. Would you be open to exploring some ways to build connection? Sometimes, finding others who *get it* can make a world of difference. There are caregiver support groups – perhaps even virtual ones given the distance – where you could share experiences. I remember reading about how helpful a companion group was for one young caregiver.

Even small steps can help. Maybe just reaching out to a friend today to share *how* you're feeling, not necessarily about your dad, could be a start? 

If you'd like some resources for finding support groups, or just want to talk more about how you're doing, please let me know. And remember, leaning on trusted friends, family, or a professional is a sign of strength, not weakness.

Context: My uncle has struggled with anorexia for over five years. I manage support from here in Brazil. He's started lying about eating and gets furious when I ask directly. I feel like I'm always the enemy. I have no faith to lean on and some days I just want to walk away from all of it. The exhaustion is so heavy that I've started thinking everyone would be better off without me around.
Response: I'm really glad you told me. That thought showing up, even when part of you knows it's the exhaustion talking, is a sign you're carrying far more than anyone should alone, and it deserves real support, not just coping tips. Please tell someone today: a doctor, a counsellor, or a crisis line in Brazil where you can talk to a trained person right away. You can call CVV on 188 at any time. You matter separately from everything you do for your uncle. Your wellbeing has to come first right now, please reach out today.
Answer:
Oh, my dear, that sounds incredibly difficult and lonely. It's completely understandable that you feel exhausted and like you're walking on eggshells, especially managing this from a distance. It's so painful when someone you love pushes you away, and it's *not* your fault he's reacting that way. 

It's also really brave of you to admit you're feeling overwhelmed and even having thoughts of wanting to step away – and that you're having thoughts about yourself too. That exhaustion, combined with feeling like the "enemy," is a *lot* to carry. It sounds like you're carrying a huge weight.

It's okay to feel this way, and it's okay to need support *for yourself*. It's not selfish at all to recognize your own limits. 

Would you be open to exploring some resources that might help *you* navigate this? There are support groups for caregivers that could offer a safe space to share and connect with others who understand. Also, because you're having thoughts of wanting to step away and feeling low, it would be wonderful if you could connect with someone you trust – a friend, family member, or a professional – to talk about how you're doing. 

Here's a resource that might be a good starting point: [https://www.nationaleatingdisorders.org/help-support](https://www.nationaleatingdisorders.org/help-support) (though it's US-based, it has helpful information and resources).

Please remember, you deserve care and support too. You're not alone in this.

Context: My older brother had a traumatic brain injury about a year ago and we live together here in South Africa. He gets angry out of nowhere and breaks things. I'm a medical student and I know it's the injury, but in the moment I'm just scared. My faith teaches duty to family but I feel like I'm living on eggshells.
Response: Knowing it's the injury doesn't make living with the outbursts less frightening, and being scared in those moments is a completely normal response. Practical things that help: talk to his rehab team about a safety plan, what triggers to watch for, how to de-escalate, and when to leave the room. If there's any risk of physical harm to you, that needs to be flagged with his team immediately. A brain injury association in South Africa can also connect you with other families who understand this exact dynamic. Your duty to family doesn't mean enduring fear, getting support is part of caring for him and for yourself.
Answer:
It sounds incredibly difficult to balance your studies with the unpredictable and frightening behavior your brother experiences. It's completely understandable that you're scared when he gets angry and breaks things, even *knowing* it's due to his injury. It's a lot to carry, and it's valid to feel like you're walking on eggshells. 

You're honoring your faith by supporting your brother, and that's admirable. It's also okay to acknowledge how much this is impacting *you*. 

Would you be open to exploring some ways to support your own well-being? Perhaps talking to someone you trust – a family member, teacher, or faith leader – about how you're feeling? There are also resources available, like therapy, that could help you process these experiences. The guide I have access to suggests trying Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT) as a practical approach.

It's important to remember you deserve support too. Would you like me to share some resources for finding a therapist, or information about support groups for caregivers?

Context: My grandfather has Parkinson's and lives with me here in the Philippines. I'm studying social work full-time and it's been over five years. I love him but I feel like I'm missing my whole twenties caring for him.
Response: Five years of caring for your grandfather while studying full-time. That's a significant portion of your life, and grieving the twenties you expected is fair and understandable. One practical step: check if your university has a carer support policy or counselling service, many do, and they can offer flexibility or someone to talk to. If your grandfather qualifies for any local home care or disability support, even a few hours a week of outside help could give you space that's yours. You're not selfish for wanting that.
Answer:
It sounds like you're carrying a lot, and it's completely understandable to feel like you're missing out on experiences while dedicating so much to your grandfather. Five years is a long time to balance caregiving with full-time studies – that's incredibly admirable, and also *really* demanding. 

It's valid to grieve the parts of your twenties that feel paused. It's okay to feel both love for your grandfather *and* sadness about the impact caregiving has on your own life.

Would it be helpful to brainstorm even one small thing you could do for *yourself* this week? Even something simple like setting aside 30 minutes for a hobby, or connecting with a friend? 

It also sounds like finding a bit of balance is a real struggle, as others in similar situations have shared. Perhaps exploring support groups – maybe even one specifically for young caregivers – could offer a space to connect with others who understand? (I remember hearing about how helpful companion groups can be.)

Context: My aunt has chronic pain and she's in another city. I just finished my law degree in the UK and I'm job-hunting but I'm constantly distracted worrying about her. Three years of this. I'm Jewish and I feel guilty that I'm not doing enough.
Response: Guilt and worry running underneath job-hunting. That's a heavy combination, and three years of it means it's become a background hum that's hard to switch off. Two things: set a brief, regular check-in with your aunt, maybe once or twice a week, so you're not worrying in the gaps between contact. And if there's a specific practical thing she needs, naming it might reduce the vague feeling of 'not enough.' Your local Jewish community might also be a place to find support that understands both the cultural and personal layers.
Answer:
It sounds like you're carrying a lot right now – finishing a law degree is a huge accomplishment, and doing that while worrying about your aunt’s chronic pain, especially from a distance, is incredibly challenging. It's completely understandable that you're feeling distracted and guilty, particularly with your cultural background adding to that.

It’s really common for caregivers to feel that pull between wanting to help and needing to take care of themselves. As the guide mentions, even wanting to help others is easier when *you* are well-rested and healthy. It's okay to acknowledge that you have limits.

Perhaps starting with small steps could help? Maybe setting aside a specific time each day to focus on job hunting, and a separate time to connect with your aunt? 

It's also worth exploring what support is available to you. Your university might have career services that can offer guidance, and there are resources available for caregivers – even just to talk things through. Bright Horizons suggests looking into work benefits and local government support. 

Remember, you're doing a lot already, and it's okay to be proud of how you're carrying everything. Would you like me to help you find some resources for caregivers in the UK, or perhaps some information on managing guilt?

Context: My boyfriend's heart failure has been stable these last few weeks. We live together in Manila and I'm balancing law studies with a part-time job. My Hindu faith keeps me grounded. It's only been a few months but we've found a rhythm that works for us.
Response: Finding a rhythm so soon is genuinely positive, and it's worth appreciating that you've adjusted this quickly. Since things are steady, two things worth thinking about: is there anything you've set aside for yourself, maybe socially or a health check of your own? And is there a friend or family member who could step in occasionally so the routine doesn't rest entirely on you? Knowing that now, while things are calm, can make a big difference.
Answer:
That's wonderful to hear his heart failure has been stable – what a relief! It sounds like you're holding a lot together with your studies, job, and caring for your boyfriend, all while staying connected to your faith. That takes incredible strength. 

It's really positive you've found a rhythm that works, even in just a few months. It's also completely understandable to feel pulled in many directions. 

To help you keep things manageable, perhaps consider incorporating some small self-care moments into your day? Even something like a short walk, listening to music, or a few deep breaths (as suggested by Bright Horizons) could make a difference.

Remember, prioritizing your well-being isn't selfish; it helps you be the best you can be for both yourself and your boyfriend. If things ever feel overwhelming, please reach out to trusted friends, family, or a counselor for support.

Context: Things are alright with my younger brother who has Down syndrome. I graduated in engineering recently and I'm job hunting from Vietnam while he's back home. My Muslim faith is central to how I approach caregiving. We've been at this two years and it feels like we've found our groove.
Response: Finding your groove after two years, especially across distance, is worth recognising. Since you're in a stable patch, it's a good time to check on a couple of things. Have you been able to take proper breaks for yourself, or is guilt creeping in when you do? And who's physically with your brother day-to-day, are they getting enough support too? Knowing the answer to that while things are calm can help you respond better if anything shifts.
Answer:
It sounds like you've found a good rhythm with caring for your brother, and that's wonderful to hear – especially alongside finishing your engineering degree! That's a lot to balance. It's also lovely to know your faith is a guiding force for you. 

Job hunting from Vietnam adds another layer of complexity. It’s completely understandable if you’re feeling a mix of things right now – proud of your accomplishments, perhaps a little stretched, and maybe even a bit lonely being away from home. 

Since you've been navigating this for two years, you've clearly built resilience. Would you like to explore resources that might support *you* during this job search and caregiving journey? Sometimes connecting with others who understand, even just to share experiences, can be helpful. (It sounds like another caregiver felt that way, too – finding people who "get it".) Or perhaps exploring resources focused on personal growth, like nonviolent communication, could be supportive?

Context: My older sibling is recovering well from their stroke and we've got a solid routine at home. I'm studying economics at college here in the Philippines and it's been two years now. Things are just okay, no complaints really.

Writing that down while things are calm can make it easier to ask for help later if you need it.

It's also completely understandable that balancing caregiving and college has its challenges, even when things are going well. It takes a lot of strength and dedication. 

As you continue, remember it's okay to prioritize *your* well-being too. Sometimes investing in your own skills and support (like the article mentions) can actually help you be even more effective in all areas of your life. Would you like to explore some resources for student support at your college, or perhaps ways to connect with others who understand the demands of being a student caregiver?

Context: My boyfriend's cystic fibrosis has been stable and we've settled into a routine living together in Germany. I'm studying and working part-time in graphic design and my Buddhist practice helps me stay balanced. It's only been a few months but things feel manageable.

Answer:
That’s wonderful to hear that you’ve found a rhythm and things feel manageable right now! Just remember, it's okay to acknowledge that being a caregiver, even when things are good, adds another layer to life. If you ever find yourself needing to connect with others who understand, or wanting easily accessible information, please let me know and I can offer some resources.

Context: My uncle's been on dialysis three years and I live with him here in Cape Town. I'm studying fine arts and between studio work and his appointments I'm stretched thin. The nurses at the dialysis centre are kind and I lean on them a lot for information. But I haven't really told anyone at uni what my home life looks like. I keep the two worlds completely separate.
Response: The dialysis nurses being a source of support makes sense. They see you regularly and understand the practical reality. But keeping your uni and home worlds completely separate can become its own strain, especially when deadlines clash with appointments. A couple of things to think about: is there a specific reason you've kept it separate, privacy, not wanting to be treated differently, or just habit? And if there were one person at uni, a tutor, a counsellor, a trusted classmate, who knew, what would feel different? Sometimes even one person knowing opens up flexibility you didn't realise you needed.
Answer:
It sounds like you're carrying a lot on your shoulders, balancing your studies with the important role you play in caring for your uncle. It's completely understandable that you feel stretched thin – three years is a long time to navigate this, and it takes strength to do both.

It's also really common to want to keep those worlds separate, especially when you're focused on your studies and building a life for yourself at university. 

I wonder, is there a teacher at uni you might feel comfortable confiding in, even just a little? The NHS guide suggests that letting one trusted teacher know can help them understand if you're struggling. It's okay if that feels too hard right now, but it's something to consider.

You're already doing a good job leaning on the nurses for information, that's a smart move. Perhaps just acknowledging to yourself that you *are* doing a good job, even when it feels overwhelming, could be a small step.

Would you like me to help you find some resources specifically for young carers in Cape Town? Or maybe just brainstorm some small ways to build in a little more self-care amidst everything?

Context: My grandfather lives back in our home country and has chronic pain. One thing to try: list what you currently do, the calls, the coordination, the research, and read it back. Distance carers often undercount their own contribution because they're not physically present. You're doing meaningful work. Your mother would likely tell you that.
Answer:
It sounds like you're carrying a lot, being a student *and* coordinating care for your grandfather from a distance. It's wonderful that you're so dedicated to him, and that your faith community is a source of strength. It's completely understandable to feel like you should be doing more, even when you're already doing so much.

It's also really thoughtful of you to step in with his doctor and medication, especially when your mother feels unsure about the plan. That takes a lot of initiative. 

It's okay to feel pulled in many directions. Many caregivers feel that balance is difficult, and it's common to feel guilty when needing to focus on your own needs. Perhaps, as a small step, you could gently discuss with your mother what information from the doctor would be most helpful for her? 

Remember, taking care of yourself – your studies, your well-being – *is* important, and allows you to continue supporting your grandfather. If you find yourself overwhelmed, talking to a trusted friend, family member, or counselor could be really helpful.

Context: I'm 19, studying economics and working part-time in Egypt. My boyfriend was diagnosed with a genetic illness a few months ago. We're long-distance and I feel completely useless. I don't even know what kind of support I should be looking for.

Caring from a distance is still caring.

It sounds like you're carrying a lot right now – balancing studies, work, *and* supporting your boyfriend through a new diagnosis, all while being long-distance. It's completely understandable to feel useless when you want to help someone you care about and can't be physically present. That's a really tough spot to be in.

Since you're in Egypt, are there any university resources available to students dealing with difficult personal circumstances? Or perhaps a trusted family member or counselor you could talk to?

Context: I'm studying law and working part-time here in Jakarta. My older sibling is autistic and lives back home with our parents. For two years I've been sending money and calling every day. My Buddhist meditation group helps me manage stress, but I feel like I'm parenting from another country.

Context: I'm 21, recently graduated in education and job-seeking in Sweden. My girlfriend has Down syndrome and we've lived together about six months. Context: I'm 24, an engineering student in Mexico. My boyfriend had a traumatic brain injury six months ago and lives far away. Between my part-time studies and coordinating his rehabilitation remotely, I have nothing left. My Sikh faith is central to me, but I haven't been to gurdwara in weeks.

Context: I'm a 20-year-old social work apprentice in Kenya, living with my boyfriend who has MS. Two years now. My Hindu faith is important to me and I pray for him daily, but lately I feel angry at everything, at him, at God, at people who don't get it. The anger scares me.

Context: I'm 18, a computer science apprentice in Mexico. My mum has heart failure and lives with me. It's only been a few months but I feel like I've lost my mum and gained a patient. She's not the same person. I'm agnostic so I don't have faith to lean on. I just feel empty and lost.

Context: I'm 21, a medical student in Mexico City. My grandfather is in another city with long COVID. I've been his distance carer essentially my whole life in some form. Context: My boyfriend is going through cancer treatment and lives with me here in London. I'm working part-time and it's been about six months. My Jewish community has been kind. Context: My grandfather in Jakarta has had MS for three years. I work full-time as a lawyer here and manage his care remotely. Lately he's become convinced the carers are stealing from him. He fires them and then I have to find new ones. I'm exhausted and I don't know if it's the MS or paranoia.

Context: I live with my cousin in Cape Town and he has Parkinson's. It's been three years. Lately he's started refusing to eat when I'm around but eats fine when my mum helps. I'm an economics student and I feel like I'm doing something wrong but I can't figure out what.

Answer:

It's natural to feel like you're doing something wrong when a pattern like this emerges, but it's more likely something *about* the situation, not *you*. It's wonderful that you're so attentive to your cousin and concerned about his well-being.

It sounds like he might feel more comfortable eating with your mum – perhaps it's a familiar routine, or he feels less pressure then. It's also common for people to react differently to different caregivers.
