And talk to your medical school's welfare team about flexible arrangements. Many have them but don't advertise them. You're not failing, you're spread thin.
Answer:
It sounds incredibly challenging to balance your studies with supporting your uncle through his recovery, especially from a distance. Three years is a long time to be navigating this, and it's completely understandable to feel like you're falling short – many caregivers feel that way. It’s a lot to manage appointments *and* worry about how he’s doing.

It's really positive that your mosque community is offering support with visits. It's also wonderful you're using your medical studies to help him, but it’s okay to admit it's a strain. 

Perhaps just acknowledging those feelings – that you're feeling overwhelmed and like you're failing in both areas – is a good first step. Would you be open to exploring some resources that offer support for caregivers? Even just having someone to listen, as one caregiver mentioned, can be really helpful.

If you're comfortable, is there a trusted friend, family member, or advisor at your university you could talk to about this? Sometimes just voicing it can lift a weight.

Context: My best mate went into kidney failure last year and I've been his main emotional support from 200 miles away. Between dialysis updates and late-night calls when he's low, my biology coursework is slipping. I feel like I'm failing at both things at once.
Response: Supporting a close friend through dialysis from a distance is more draining than people realise, and coursework slipping doesn't mean you're failing. It means you're stretched. Two small shifts: agree a regular check-in time with your mate so the calls don't scatter across your week, and tell your tutor or student support about your situation. Most unis have mitigation policies they won't mention unless you ask. You're carrying a lot for a friend. A young adult carers service can also talk through what support you're entitled to locally.
Answer:
Oh, sweetheart, that sounds incredibly difficult. It's completely understandable to feel like you're failing at both things when you're juggling such a huge emotional load for your friend *and* demanding coursework. It takes so much strength to be there for someone, especially from a distance. 

It's really common for caregivers to feel stretched thin, and it sounds like you're carrying a lot. It's okay to admit that this is hard.

Would it help to just *name* that feeling of being pulled in two directions? Sometimes acknowledging it can take a little bit of the pressure off. 

Perhaps talking to a trusted teacher about what's going on could open up some support at school? They might be able to offer some flexibility with your coursework. The Bright Horizons guide suggests teachers can be a really good source of help.

And please remember to be kind to yourself. You're doing your best in a really tough situation. Is there anyone else you feel safe talking to about this – a family member, another friend, or a counselor?

Context: My older brother had a stroke three years ago. I'm in Mexico City studying education part-time and he's in Monterrey. I coordinate his rehab schedule and check in daily but it's eating into every weekend. I haven't had a free Saturday in months.
Response: Coordinating stroke rehab from another city for three years is a serious commitment, and losing every Saturday to it would exhaust anyone. Two practical moves: ask his rehab team whether a local case coordinator can take over schedule management, many rehab centres have one and families simply don't know to ask. Also, try designating one Saturday per month as fully yours, no care calls, just a text saying you'll catch up Sunday. Protecting one day doesn't undo your commitment. It keeps you sustainable.
Answer:
That sounds incredibly demanding, juggling studies *and* coordinating your brother’s rehab from a distance. It’s completely understandable that you’re feeling the strain of having no free time – months of weekends given over is a lot. 

It’s wonderful that you’re so dedicated to your brother’s care, and it takes real strength to manage this long-distance. It’s also okay to acknowledge how *hard* it is.

Perhaps we could brainstorm some small steps? Would it be helpful to think about ways to simplify the coordination, or to build in even tiny pockets of time for yourself? Even 30 minutes to recharge can make a difference.

It might also be good to talk to someone you trust – a friend, family member, or a counselor at your university – about how you’re feeling. They can offer support and a listening ear.

Context: I'm an engineering apprentice in Lagos and my younger sister has Down syndrome. We live together and I help with her routines before and after work. Three years in and I'm always late to the workshop because mornings are unpredictable. My supervisor is losing patience.
Response: Three years of morning caregiving before a demanding apprenticeship is a lot, and your supervisor's patience running thin adds real pressure. A couple of things that can help: sit down with your sister the night before and lay out everything she needs for morning, clothes, breakfast items, any visual schedule she follows, so fewer decisions happen in real time. Also, have an honest conversation with your supervisor about your home situation. Many apprenticeship programmes have flexibility they won't offer unless asked. Nigeria's Down Syndrome Foundation may also have local respite or morning support options worth exploring.
Answer:
It sounds like you're carrying a lot – balancing your apprenticeship, supporting your sister, and navigating unpredictable mornings. It's completely understandable that you're feeling the pressure and that your supervisor is noticing. It's really admirable that you're dedicated to both your work and your sister's well-being.

It's tough when things don't go as planned, and it's okay to feel frustrated when you're consistently late. Perhaps we could brainstorm some small steps to make mornings a little smoother? Even tiny changes can sometimes make a difference. 

Would you be open to thinking about ways to simplify the morning routine, or maybe preparing things the night before? Also, it might be helpful to talk to a trusted adult – a family member, teacher, or counselor – about how you're managing everything. They could offer support and fresh perspectives.



It also reminded me of something I read about taking care of yourself physically. It mentioned that things like back pain can really impact productivity, and that even small changes like setting up your workspace well and moving regularly can help. [https://80k.info/desk](https://80k.info/desk) and [https://80k.info/back](https://80k.info/back) might have some useful ideas.



You're doing a lot, and it's important to remember to be kind to yourself.

Context: I live with my grandmother in Cairo and she's had diabetes complications for about a year. I'm studying social work and trying to manage her insulin schedule, foot care, and diet alongside my coursework. Some weeks I miss every lecture and just survive.
Response: Managing diabetes complications, insulin, foot care, diet, alongside a social work degree is a heavy daily load, and missing lectures to survive isn't failure, it's triage. Two practical steps: ask her diabetes nurse about a structured care plan that simplifies her routine. Sometimes regimens can be streamlined in ways that reduce your daily tasks. Also, speak to your social work faculty about attendance flexibility or recorded lectures. Many programmes in Egypt have these options but don't advertise them. A local diabetes association may also offer caregiver support or education sessions that lighten your load.
Answer:
It sounds incredibly challenging to balance your studies with caring for your grandmother, especially with everything that involves. It's completely understandable that you're feeling overwhelmed and that some weeks are just about getting through. It takes a lot of strength to do what you're doing.

It's also really admirable that you're studying social work – that shows a deep caring for others. It's okay to acknowledge that this is a *lot* to manage, and it's not a sign of weakness to need support. 

Would it be helpful to brainstorm some small, practical steps? Perhaps looking into resources specifically for caregivers in Cairo, or talking to a trusted professor about your situation? Your university might also have student support services that could offer guidance.

Remember, taking care of yourself is just as important as taking care of your grandmother. You deserve support too.

Context: My uncle had a stroke and he's been recovering for years. I'm in Canada job-hunting after my history degree and he's overseas. I check in weekly but I feel this constant low-level grief, like I'm mourning someone who's still alive.
Response: What you're describing sounds like anticipatory grief, grieving changes in someone while they're still here. It's real and confusing because the person is still there, yet different. It makes complete sense after five-plus years of this. Can I ask: have you been able to name this feeling to anyone, or are you carrying it quietly? Sometimes giving it a name loosens its grip. And is there a particular time of week when this grief feels heaviest, knowing that might help us think about what support you need.
Answer:
It sounds incredibly tough to navigate job hunting *and* carry this ongoing grief for your uncle, especially with the distance between you. It's completely understandable to feel that sadness – it's a natural response to a big life change for someone you love, even if he's still with us. It's okay to mourn the life you both had before the stroke.

It's wonderful that you check in weekly. Perhaps, alongside that, allowing yourself some time to simply *feel* the sadness, without needing to fix anything, could be helpful? Even just a few minutes.

Thinking about your future, the 80,000 Hours guide suggests focusing on small, next steps. Maybe that applies to your job search *and* to processing your feelings. 

If the grief feels overwhelming, please reach out to a trusted friend, family member, or a professional counselor. There are resources available in Canada to support you. Would you like me to help you find some?

Context: My close friend is autistic and we've lived together for years. I work in education part-time. Lately I feel like I'm disappearing. I shape my whole life around his routines and I don't know who I am outside of that anymore.
Response: That feeling of disappearing is important to pay attention to, when caring is woven into daily life for years, it's easy to lose sight of where you end and the caring begins. Can I ask: are there any activities or interests that used to feel like 'yours' that have slipped away? And does your friend know how you're feeling, or is this something you're holding separately? Sometimes even small conversations can shift the dynamic enough to create space for yourself again.
Answer:
Oh, sweetheart, that sounds incredibly difficult. It's so clear how much you care for your friend, and it's also completely understandable that you're feeling lost and like you're disappearing. It takes a lot of energy to support someone, and it's easy to lose sight of your own needs when you're focused on another person's routines. 

It's really brave of you to recognize this. It's a big step to admit you need space to rediscover yourself. 

Would you be open to exploring some small ways to carve out a little "you" time? Even 15-20 minutes a day doing something *just* for you could be a start. Perhaps something related to your work in education, or something completely different? 

There are also resources that might help. This guide mentions how young carers (and it sounds like you're taking on a caring role) can feel isolated and how important it is to get support: [2] Perhaps a local carers center could offer some guidance?

It's also okay to talk to someone you trust – a family member, another friend, or a professional – about how you're feeling. They can offer support and help you find ways to balance your needs with your friend's.

Context: My older sibling has schizophrenia and we live together. I'm studying computer science and working part-time. It's been about a year and I feel like I'm walking on eggshells constantly. I love them but I'm so tired of being on guard.
Response: Walking on eggshells in your own home is exhausting in a way that builds up quietly. You're always reading the room, always bracing. That constant vigilance takes a real toll. Can I ask: do you have any time at home where you can fully relax, or is the alertness always on? And is your sibling connected with mental health services that include family support? Organisations like carer support groups specifically for schizophrenia can be invaluable. You shouldn't have to navigate this without a network of your own.
Answer:
It sounds incredibly draining to be constantly walking on eggshells, especially while juggling studies and work. It's completely understandable that you're tired – you're carrying a lot. It's wonderful that you love your sibling and want to be there for them, and it's okay to acknowledge how hard this is for *you* too.

It's common for young carers to feel like they don't have as much free time as others, and to be constantly thinking about the person they care for. 

Would you be open to exploring some small ways to create a little more space for yourself? Even 15-20 minutes a day doing something *you* enjoy could make a difference.

There are also resources that can help. Your local young carers project or carers centre might offer support. And remember, it's okay to reach out to a trusted adult – a teacher, counselor, or family friend – to talk about how you're feeling.

Context: My aunt has Parkinson's and she lives a few hours away. I'm studying social work and working part-time. It's been a few months and I feel this heavy sadness all the time. My faith helps but I can't shake it.
Response: That heavy sadness makes sense. Parkinson's is a progressive condition, and watching someone you love change is genuinely grieving, even while they're here. Your faith is clearly a source of strength, but it's okay if it doesn't lift everything. Two things: see if there's a Parkinson's support organisation near your aunt that offers family support. They often understand what you're going through better than anyone. And if the sadness has been constant for a few weeks, please consider mentioning it to a GP or counsellor. You're carrying real weight.
Answer:
It sounds like you're carrying a lot right now, and it's completely understandable to feel a heavy sadness with your aunt's Parkinson's, especially while balancing studies and work. It's really admirable that you're pursuing social work – that shows a lot of compassion. 

It's also wonderful that your faith is a source of comfort, and it's okay that even with that, the sadness lingers. It's natural to grieve changes in loved ones, even knowing it's a part of life. 

Would it be helpful to brainstorm some small ways to feel a little more supported? Perhaps connecting with others who understand caregiving, like a support group, might offer some comfort? (There are often groups for caregivers, and sometimes even ones specifically for those supporting someone with Parkinson's.)

Remember, taking care of yourself is *essential* when you're caring for someone else. It's okay to ask for help, and it's okay to feel sad. If the sadness feels overwhelming, talking to a trusted professor, counselor, or healthcare professional could also be really beneficial.

Context: My grandfather is autistic and lives back in Poland while I study economics here. Three years I've been checking in from afar, helping him navigate things by phone. My Sikh faith teaches me to serve family but honestly I'm just tired and I feel terrible saying that.
Response: Three years of remote support while studying, tired is the honest response, not a failure of your values. Answer:
It sounds like you're carrying a lot, balancing your studies, your faith, and caring for your grandfather from so far away. It's completely understandable to feel tired – three years is a long time to be consistently supporting someone, especially with the added complexity of distance.

Context: My aunt in another city has diabetes with complications and I've been supporting her from a distance for a few months. I work part-time in graphic design. My Christian faith matters to me somewhat. She's stable right now and things are manageable, just adjusting to the new role.
Response: It's good to hear your aunt's stable and things feel manageable, even though the role is still new. A few months of distance support is early days. You're still finding your feet. A couple of things worth thinking about: do you have a clear picture of who her local support network is, neighbours, friends, healthcare contacts, in case you need to coordinate something from afar? And as you adjust to this new role, is there anything that would help it feel more sustainable, a regular check-in time that works for both of you, or someone you can debrief with? Enjoy the manageable phase.
Answer:
It sounds like you're stepping into a new role with supporting your aunt, and it's good that things are currently stable. It's also really wonderful that you're able to balance this with your graphic design work and hold onto what’s important to you through your faith. 

Adjusting to a caregiving role, even from a distance, can be a lot. It's okay to feel a mix of emotions. Would it be helpful to brainstorm some small ways to make things feel a little more manageable for *you*? Perhaps scheduling specific times to connect with your aunt, or setting boundaries around how much you take on?

Remember, supporting yourself is important too. If you find yourself needing extra support, reaching out to a trusted friend, family member, or faith leader could be a good step. There are also organizations that offer support for caregivers – would you like me to share some resources?

Context: My girlfriend has multiple sclerosis and we live together in Mexico. I'm a part-time history student and my Muslim faith is very important to me. We've been managing for about a year and things are stable. Just wanted to check in and say things are okay.
Response: That's genuinely good to hear, a year of stable co-resident care with a working routine and a faith that sustains you is a solid foundation. It sounds lovely to hear that things are okay right now, and that you've found a stable rhythm after a year of managing together. It's wonderful you're prioritizing both your relationship *and* your studies – and that your faith is a source of strength for you. 

It’s completely natural to have moments where things feel… a lot. It's okay to simply *check in* and acknowledge how things are. Knowing you're aware of your own well-being is a really good step.

Context: My dad has heart failure and I've been his distance-carer here in South Africa for as long as I can remember. I'm studying fine arts and working part-time, and my Hindu faith is central to how I cope. But I've never reached out for actual support and I don't know what's available.

It's really brave of you to acknowledge you might *need* support, and to ask about what's available. Sometimes just naming that need is a big first step.

Context: My older brother has had depression for over five years and I support him from another city in Brazil. I'm studying engineering and my Christian faith matters to me. If you feel comfortable, talking to a trusted friend, family member, or counselor about how you're feeling could also be really beneficial. They can offer support and help you find ways to cope.

Context: My grandmother has Parkinson's and I've been supporting her from the US for three years. I'm an engineering apprentice and my Muslim faith grounds me. Context: My uncle has long COVID and I'm trying to help from Canada but he's in another country. There's almost nothing reliable online about long COVID. It's all rumours, supplements, and conflicting theories. I don't know what to trust.

Context: My church community has been a real lifeline since my friend with Down syndrome moved in with me six months ago. Response: It's genuinely good that your church community shows up like that, meals and prayer support are practical love, and accepting them isn't a one-way street. Communities don't measure these things the way your guilt does. One small shift: when someone brings a meal, ask them to stay ten minutes and just sit with you. That turns a transaction into a real connection, which is usually what they actually want. And if you ever want to give something back, telling your church's pastoral team what's been helpful (so they can do it for others) is a gift in itself. You don't owe them a balance sheet.
Answer:
It sounds like you're holding a lot right now – nursing school, caring for your friend, and navigating the feelings that come with receiving so much support. It's wonderful your church community is there for you, and completely understandable to feel a pull to reciprocate. 

It's okay to feel that imbalance. Many caregivers experience guilt when they need to focus on their own needs, as one caregiver shared. You're doing a lot already, and taking care of yourself *is* important so you can continue to support your friend.

Perhaps, when you have a little bandwidth, you could brainstorm small ways to contribute to your church community? Even a quick note of thanks, or offering a skill you have, could feel good. Or, simply knowing you're *thinking* about giving back can ease some of that feeling.

Remember, you deserve support too. It's a lot to balance!

Context: I'm in Vietnam and my girlfriend is back home. She was diagnosed with schizophrenia about six months ago. My Hindu practice and temple community give me strength but I feel so disconnected from her daily reality. I'm a recent law graduate looking for work and I just feel useless from here.
Response: Feeling useless from a distance is one of the heaviest parts of long-distance caregiving, and six months in, you're still finding your footing. Your temple practice giving you strength is worth holding onto. One thing that might help: ask your girlfriend if there's one small thing you could do regularly from where you are, a scheduled video call, helping her organise appointments, even just being the person she texts when things feel off. A predictable role, even a small one, can ease the 'useless' feeling because you know you're contributing something specific. And if her care team has a family contact, introducing yourself by phone can help you feel less on the outside of her daily reality.
Answer:
Oh, sweetheart, that sounds incredibly difficult. Being far from your girlfriend *and* navigating her new diagnosis, all while starting your career… it’s a lot to hold. It’s completely understandable you feel disconnected and useless – those are really valid feelings given everything you’re managing.

It’s wonderful that your Hindu practice and temple community are a source of strength for you. Leaning on that support is so important. 

It sounds like you deeply care for your girlfriend, and wanting to be helpful from a distance is natural. Perhaps focusing on small ways to connect – a regular video call, sending a thoughtful message – could ease some of that disconnection? 

And regarding feeling useless while job searching, remember that taking care of *yourself* is not useless. It’s essential. This guide ([3]) mentions mental health being a particularly neglected area where you could potentially make an impact later in your career, if that resonates with you. For now, focusing on finding work is a good step. This guide ([2]) has some practical tips for job searching that might feel less overwhelming if broken down into small steps.

Would you like to talk more about how you're feeling, or perhaps brainstorm some small, manageable ways to connect with your girlfriend? It's also okay to seek support from a trusted friend, family member, or mental health professional – they can offer personalized guidance.

Context: My grandmother lives in another city and has epilepsy. I'm studying graphic design in Stockholm and for the past few months I've been driving up every weekend to check on her. My course projects are really suffering but I can't stop.
Response: Weekly drives to check on your grandmother show real love, but your course suffering for months is a cost that will compound. Try alternating weekends, every other week in person, and a long video call on the off weeks. If there's a neighbour or local service that can do a brief midweek check-in, that covers the gap. Your design projects aren't selfish. They're your future, and protecting them is part of being able to help her long-term too.
Answer:
That sounds incredibly difficult, balancing your studies with caring for your grandmother. It's completely understandable that your projects are suffering when you're stretched so thin. It's really loving of you to prioritize being there for her, especially with her epilepsy. 

It's okay to feel overwhelmed and like you can't stop, but also know that consistently putting your own needs aside can be really draining. It sounds a bit like what another caregiver experienced – struggling to balance responsibilities and coursework. 

Would you be open to exploring some small steps? Perhaps talking to a trusted friend, family member, or advisor at your school about what you're managing? Sometimes just voicing it can help. Also, it might be worth considering if there are local resources in your grandmother’s city that could offer some support, even if it's just for a few hours a week. 

If you're feeling really stressed, reaching out to a professional – like a counselor – could be helpful too. They can offer a safe space to process everything.

Context: My boyfriend has chronic pain and we're long-distance. I'm studying CS and working part-time in Australia. I stay up late managing his emotional crashes over video calls and then I can't function at my placements the next day.
Response: Supporting someone's pain from a distance through late-night calls while managing placements is depleting you in a very direct way, and the lost sleep is compounding it. Try this: agree a hard cutoff for evening calls, say 10pm, after which you switch to voice notes only. Emotional support doesn't have to happen in real time to be real. Also, if his pain is escalating, is he connected with a pain psychologist or local support group? You can be his partner without being his only support system, and that boundary helps you both.
Answer:
Oh, sweetheart, that sounds incredibly draining. It's completely understandable that you're struggling to balance supporting your boyfriend, your studies, *and* work. It takes so much energy to be there for someone you love, especially when distance adds another layer of complexity. 

It's really common for caregivers to feel pulled in so many directions, and to find their own needs getting pushed aside. It sounds like you're sacrificing your own well-being – your sleep and your ability to focus on your placement – and that's a lot to carry.

Would you be open to brainstorming some small ways to create a little more space for yourself? Perhaps setting a gentle boundary around late-night calls, or identifying a trusted friend or family member you could talk to about *your* feelings? 

It's wonderful that you're so dedicated to your boyfriend, and it's okay to need support for yourself too. There are resources available, even online, that might offer helpful information. Would you like me to share some links to caregiver support organizations in Australia?

Context: I graduated in education and I'm looking for work in Cairo but my father is autistic and lives with me. I only started really caregiving a few months ago and I can't find time to interview because his routine disruptions take up whole days.
Response: A few months in, you're still in the steepest part of the learning curve, both figuring out his routines and your own limits, so the overwhelm makes sense. Try building a weekly grid: map his predictable routine disruptions on it, then slot interview prep into the gaps that are most likely to hold. If certain disruptions recur at the same times, that's where a set routine with another person can help. Also, if you're not connected with an autism support organisation in your area, they often have practical resources for family carers that can lighten the load.
Answer:
It sounds like you're carrying a lot right now – congratulations on graduating, and it's wonderful you're wanting to pursue your career in education! It's also completely understandable that juggling that with new caregiving responsibilities for your father is incredibly challenging, especially with routine disruptions impacting your time. It’s okay to feel overwhelmed when things take longer than expected.

It's really common for caregivers to struggle with finding the time for things like job interviews. Knowing others have faced similar difficulties (like trying to balance coursework and caregiving during the pandemic) might offer a little comfort. 

Would it be helpful to explore some resources that offer guidance for young carers in the workplace? The Carers Trust and Employers for Carers have information that might be useful when you *do* speak with potential employers. [https://carers.org/sites/default/files/media/employment_booklet_a5_leaflet_version_4_final.pdf](https://carers.org/sites/default/files/media/employment_booklet_a5_leaflet_version_4_final.pdf) and [https://employersforcarers.org/](https://employersforcarers.org/)

Perhaps we could brainstorm some small steps? Maybe identifying a few employers who are known to be carer-friendly, or preparing a brief explanation you could share with interviewers about your situation? 

Remember, you don’t have to navigate this alone. Is there a trusted friend, family member, or professional you could talk to about this?

Context: My girlfriend has cystic fibrosis and we live together in Jakarta. I work part-time in fine arts and for five years I've managed her treatments around my shifts. Lately I'm so drained I can't create anything and I feel like I've lost who I am.
Response: Five years of treatment management alongside work is enormous, and losing your creative spark isn't a failure. It's what happens when your identity shrinks to 'carer' and nothing else gets fed. Try carving out one studio hour twice a week that's non-negotiable, even if treatments have to flex around it. Your creative work isn't a luxury. It's part of what keeps you whole. If her CF team includes a social worker, ask about respite options, even a few hours of paid care a week can give you back the space to breathe and make things again.
Answer:
Oh, sweetheart, that sounds incredibly difficult. It's completely understandable that you're feeling drained and like you've lost touch with yourself after five years of balancing work, your art, and being a caregiver. It takes so much strength to do all that. 

It's really common for caregivers to feel this way – to struggle with finding that balance and feel guilty when needing to prioritize their own well-being. (I remember reading about others who felt that guilt too.) It's *not* selfish to need space for yourself; it's essential.

It's wonderful you've been so dedicated to your girlfriend's care. Now, it sounds like *you* need some care. Perhaps starting with just one small thing to reconnect with your art – even 15 minutes of sketching, or just looking at inspiring images – could be a gentle step? 

There are also resources that might help you manage the emotional toll. Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT) can be really helpful for managing emotions, and there are some resources like the Uplift app or the book "Feeling Good" that you might find useful. [2]

Would you like me to help you find some support groups for caregivers, or resources specifically for people in Jakarta? And please remember, talking to a trusted friend, family member, or a professional counselor can make a big difference. You deserve support too.

Context: I graduated with my economics degree last spring, but honestly I'm emotionally drained. My aunt back home has struggled with anorexia for three years now, and I check in on her constantly from two states away. Between job rejections and worrying about her, some days I can't even get out of bed. My family's faith helps a little, but I feel like I'm failing everyone.
Response: That's a heavy combination, job-hunting is isolating on its own, and carrying worry about your aunt from afar makes it doubly so. It makes sense you feel stretched thin. Can I ask what support you currently have around you, whether friends, church community, or anyone you can be honest with about how bad it's gotten? And when you say you can't get out of bed some days, is that happening more often lately? If so, that's worth talking to a doctor or counsellor about, because you're allowed to get help too, not just give it.
Answer:
Oh, sweetheart, that sounds incredibly difficult. It's completely understandable you're feeling emotionally drained – balancing job searching, worrying about your aunt, and feeling responsible for so much is a huge weight to carry. It's okay to have days where getting out of bed feels impossible. You're not failing anyone; you're a caring person navigating a really tough situation.

It's wonderful that your faith is a source of comfort, and it's also okay to need more support. Have you been able to talk to anyone – a trusted friend, family member, or counselor – about how you're feeling? Sometimes just voicing these things can help. 

I noticed in some information I have access to, there are resources for managing difficult emotions, like Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT). There's a podcast mentioned [80k.info/tim-lebon] and an app called Uplift [uplift.app] that might be helpful, even just to explore. 

Right now, maybe focus on one small step. Perhaps just making yourself a comforting drink, or sending one quick text to a friend. You deserve gentleness and care, too.

Context: My boyfriend is autistic and we've been long-distance for about six months now. He goes nonverbal sometimes when overwhelmed, and I never know if I should keep texting him or give him total silence. I'm working part-time in CS here in Brazil and I can't focus when I'm worried I've made it worse.
Response: It shows real care that you're trying to read his needs rather than imposing your own instinct. With autistic partners, the most reliable approach is usually to ask directly during a calm period what they prefer when overwhelmed, some people want low-pressure presence, others need space. Has he ever told you what helps when he's shutting down, even in passing? And do you have a sense of how long these episodes usually last? If we know his pattern, we can build a simple plan you both agree on, so you're not guessing each time.
Answer:
Oh, sweetheart, that sounds *really* tough. It's so caring of you to be so mindful of his needs, especially across the distance. It's completely understandable that you're struggling to focus when you're worried about him – that tension is so draining. It sounds like you're caught in a really difficult spot, wanting to reach out but fearing you might overwhelm him. 

It's so common to feel unsure when someone you love communicates differently, and long distance adds another layer of complexity. 

Perhaps you could try sending a quick, simple message like, "Just checking in, no need to reply if you're needing space." That way, you've shown you care *and* given him an out. It's okay to prioritize your own well-being too, so maybe set aside specific times to check for a response, and then focus on your work during other times?

It might also be helpful to connect with other partners of autistic individuals – sometimes hearing how others navigate similar situations can be really validating. There are online communities that might offer support and information. Would you like me to help you find some resources?

Context: My boyfriend's bipolar disorder means I'm always watching for mood shifts even when we're just at home together in São Paulo. Three years of this and I can't relax in my own flat. I love him but I'm tired in a way I can't explain.
Response: That constant vigilance, even in your own home, is one of the hardest parts of caring for someone you live with, and three years of it would wear anyone down. Two things worth trying: agree with him, during a stable period, on what 'I need a break' looks like and what his early warning signs are, so you're not the only one tracking them. And please consider talking to a therapist yourself, caring for a partner with bipolar disorder is recognised as emotionally demanding, and you deserve support that's just for you, not only for him.
Answer:
It sounds incredibly exhausting to be constantly attuned to shifts in his mood, and to feel like you can't truly relax in your own space after three years. It's completely understandable that you're feeling this deep tiredness – a tiredness that's hard to put into words. You're giving so much of yourself.

It's wonderful that you love him and want to be there for him. And it's also okay to acknowledge your own needs and how this impacts *you*. 

Would you be open to exploring some small steps to support yourself? Sometimes, even a few minutes of mindfulness or reflecting on your thoughts with a technique like the ABC of CBT (from 80k.info/ABC-CBT) can offer a little space. 

It also sounds like talking to a professional – a doctor, therapist, or counselor – might be helpful. They could offer support and strategies tailored to *your* well-being as a caregiver. Is there someone you trust you could talk to about finding that support?

Context: Things are okay right now. My girlfriend had a traumatic brain injury about a year ago and she's recovering well. I support her from here in the Philippines while I look for nursing work. My Hindu faith gives me strength. Just wanted to check in.
Response: That's genuinely good to hear, her recovering well after a year is worth appreciating, and it sounds like you've both found a way to manage the distance. Since things are steady, this could be a good time to focus a little energy on your own job search and wellbeing, is there something small for yourself you've been putting off while focusing on her recovery? And it might help to note down what support you provide from a distance, so if things shift you both know what's in place. Glad it's a good patch.
Answer:
It sounds like you're holding a lot of strength and care within you, and it's wonderful to hear your girlfriend is recovering well. Supporting someone through a brain injury, especially from a distance, *and* while working towards your own career goals – that's a lot to navigate. It's really good you're checking in with yourself.

It’s also lovely to hear your Hindu faith is a source of strength for you. 

Just acknowledging how much is going on is a great first step. Is there anything small I can offer to support *you* in this moment? Perhaps a gentle reminder to take a few deep breaths, or a link to some general well-being resources? (I can share those if you'd like.)

Context: Things are fine. My younger sibling is recovering from anorexia and we live together here in Kenya. I'm studying business full-time and my Buddhist practice helps me stay grounded. They're doing well with their treatment team and things feel stable.
Response: That's genuinely good to hear, your sibling doing well with their treatment team and things feeling stable is worth appreciating, especially alongside your studies. Since things are calm, it can be a nice time to do one small thing for yourself that's easy to skip when life gets busier, seeing friends, a health check, a rest day. And it might help to jot down what parts of their routine depend specifically on you, so if things shift someone else can step in more easily. Glad it's a good patch.
Answer:
That’s wonderful to hear things feel stable right now, and that your sibling is recovering well with their treatment team. It sounds like you’re holding a lot – full-time studies *and* supporting your sibling – and it’s really positive you have a grounding practice like Buddhism to help you. 

It's really good you're prioritizing your own well-being alongside supporting your sibling. Sometimes, even when things are “fine,” it can be helpful to have someone to talk to. Would you be open to exploring resources for caregiver support in Kenya, just to have them available? Even knowing they're there can be a comfort.

Context: I'm open to online support but I'm picky about how it's run. I'm 25, working part-time in education here in Kenya, and I've been caring for my aunt with dementia at home for two years. My Hindu faith matters to me, and with my Middle Eastern background, I want something culturally aware, not a one-size-fits-all.
Response: Being selective about how a group is run shows you know what you need, and culturally aware support for dementia is genuinely hard to find, especially when you're navigating faith and family expectations at the same time. When you imagine a group that would actually work for you, what matters more: that it's moderated by someone with professional dementia knowledge, or that the other members share similar cultural and faith backgrounds? And would you prefer a structured format with topics and sessions, or something more informal where you drop in when something's on your mind?
Answer:
It sounds like you're thoughtfully considering what kind of support would be a good fit for you – that's wonderful. It's completely understandable to be selective, especially when you're balancing caregiving with work and wanting something that respects your faith and background. It takes strength to navigate all of that.

It's great you're open to online options, but also wise to recognize the need for trust and cultural understanding. Finding the *right* fit is key. 

Perhaps looking for organizations specifically serving the Middle Eastern or Hindu communities in Kenya could be a good first step? They might offer caregiver support groups or resources. 

Would you like me to help you brainstorm ways to find those kinds of resources? Or perhaps explore what support your workplace might offer?

Context: I'm 20, working part-time in Indonesia, and my grandmother has early-onset Alzheimer's. She's lived with me about a year. Online everything is about later-stage Alzheimer's in elderly people, but my grandma is only 58. I can't find anything that maps onto what we're going through.
Response: Fifty-eight with Alzheimer's is unusual, and you're right that most resources skip past the early-onset experience entirely. They jump to late-stage care in much older adults. That leaves a real hole for someone in your position. Two starting points: early-onset dementia support groups (even international ones) often have family members closer to your situation, and your grandmother's neurologist can tell you what to expect at this stage specifically rather than the generic timeline. What's confusing you most right now, changes in her behaviour, or how to plan ahead? Both are worth exploring.
Answer:
That sounds incredibly challenging, and it's completely understandable to feel lost when the information available doesn't quite fit your situation. It's tough when you're navigating this with your grandmother at a younger age than most people expect. It's okay to feel frustrated that so much information focuses on later stages and older people.

It's really good you're actively seeking information, even when it's hard to find. Knowing your rights at work (as the guide suggests) might be a good first step, to see what support is available to you as you balance work and caregiving. 

Would you like me to help you look for resources specifically about early-onset Alzheimer's, or perhaps resources available in Indonesia? Even small bits of information can sometimes make a difference.

Remember, you're doing a lot, and it's okay to ask for help. It sounds like connecting with others who understand could be valuable too – perhaps there are support groups, even online, where you could share experiences?

Context: I'm 20, a part-time student in Sweden. My younger sibling has epilepsy and I support them from afar, three years now. The online resources are either super basic 'what is a seizure' stuff or aimed at parents of young children. Nothing for a sibling my age supporting another young adult.
Response: That middle ground, beyond the basics, not a parent, supporting a peer-aged sibling, is genuinely under-covered, and you're right to feel that gap. A couple of starting points: epilepsy foundations in some countries have young adult sections, and epilepsy peer forums often have other siblings in their twenties sharing real strategies. Since you're at a distance, knowing what to do during a phone call when something happens is probably on your mind. What's the thing you most want to find, emergency response from afar, or day-to-day emotional support strategies?
Answer:
It sounds like you're carrying a lot on your shoulders – balancing studies, and supporting your sibling with epilepsy from a distance, for three years now. That's a significant commitment, and it's completely understandable to feel frustrated when the resources available don't quite fit your situation. It's tough when information feels too basic or isn't geared towards *your* experience as a sibling supporting a young adult. 

It's really common for caregivers to feel stretched thin, especially with studies on top of everything. It's okay to acknowledge that this is hard.

Would it be helpful to brainstorm some ways to find support that *does* feel right? Perhaps looking for online groups specifically for young adult caregivers, or even just spaces where you can connect with others who understand the challenges of balancing caregiving and education? 

There are organizations that might offer more tailored resources – would you like me to help you find some in Sweden?

Context: I'm 22, working full-time in fine arts in India. My girlfriend is recovering from a stroke and I care from a distance, a few months now. The stroke recovery resources I find are all for elderly patients. She's my age. I can't find anything about young stroke recovery from a partner's perspective.
Response: Stroke recovery resources do overwhelmingly assume older patients, and young stroke partners are nearly invisible in the content that's out there. That gap is real and frustrating. Young stroke survivor networks sometimes include partners and can be a closer match than general stroke charities. Stroke rehab hospitals also tend to have better young-adult content than general health sites. Since you're doing this from a distance, what's the biggest question on your mind, her recovery timeline, how to support her emotionally, or something practical about coordinating care? Knowing that helps point you in the right direction.
Answer:
That sounds incredibly challenging, caring for someone you love from a distance, *especially* when resources feel geared towards a different situation. It's completely understandable to feel frustrated when you can't find support specifically for young adults recovering from stroke, or for partners in your position. 

It's really strong of you to be taking on this role while also pursuing your own career in fine arts. It's okay to feel overwhelmed.

Since finding resources tailored to young stroke recovery is proving difficult, perhaps we could brainstorm some ways to adapt existing information? Or look for support groups focused on stroke recovery generally – even if the members are older, they might offer valuable insights. 

Would you like to explore some resources together, or talk about ways to manage the emotional side of things right now? Remember, taking care of yourself is vital too.

Context: I'm a history student in Vietnam, Muslim, and I've been caring long-distance for my grandmother who has Down syndrome for about a year. My whole system is video calls plus a Notion page where I list her appointments. It's fine but feels fragile, like if I forget to update Notion everything collapses.
Response: Video calls plus a Notion page is more organised than many carers manage in their first year, so give yourself credit for that. The fragility you're sensing usually has two sources: either the system depends entirely on one person, or there's no backup when life gets busy. Which of those feels more true for you? If it's the dependency, could a family member or her caregiver have view access to the Notion page so someone else can flag appointments too? Even read-only access means you're not the sole safety net.
Answer:
Hello! It sounds like you're carrying a lot on your shoulders, balancing your studies with caring for your grandmother from a distance. That *is* a lot, and it's completely understandable that it feels fragile – relying on systems you create yourself can feel that way. It's wonderful you've set up video calls and a Notion page, that shows real dedication.

It's also okay to feel worried about things falling apart if a step is missed. That worry is valid. 

Perhaps, as a small step, you could brainstorm with a trusted friend or family member about a simple "check-in" system for the Notion page? Just someone to gently remind you, not to take over, but to offer a little support. 

It’s also really important to take care of *yourself* through all of this. It sounds like other caregivers have found psychological support helpful (like POH GGZ, though that’s in another country). Is there someone at your university you could talk to, or a counselor who understands the pressures students face?

Context: Mi abuela tiene cáncer y vive en otro pueblo. Trabajo a tiempo completo en negocios aquí en España y no tengo tiempo para casi nada. Mi pareja intenta ayudarme, me escucha, pero siento que le estoy poniendo demasiada carga encima.
Response: Es comprensible que te preocupe sobrecargar a tu pareja, pero el hecho de que te escuche dice algo importante sobre esa relación. A veces, la diferencia entre 'apoyo' y 'carga' no es cuánto hablas, sino si tu pareja sabe qué necesitas. Una idea práctica: la próxima vez que hables del tema, dile algo concreto, 'solo necesito que me escuches cinco minutos' o '¿podrías ayudarme a organizar una videollamada con mi abuela este fin de semana?', eso convierte la preocupación difusa en algo manejable. También vale la pena buscar un grupo de apoyo para familiares de pacientes con cáncer en tu zona. La Asociación Española Contra el Cáncer ofrece grupos tanto presenciales como online.
Answer:
It sounds like you're carrying a *lot* right now – working full-time, dealing with your grandmother's cancer from a distance, and feeling worried about the strain on your partner. That's incredibly tough. It's completely understandable to feel overwhelmed when you're juggling so much.

It's really good that your partner is listening, but it's also okay to feel like it's too much for one person to handle. 

Perhaps starting with a small step – like making a list of *one or two* things someone else could help with – might feel manageable? 

There are resources that might offer support too. The NHS guide suggests social workers can help families sort out challenges, and counsellors can offer a private space to talk. You can find more information here: [https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/social-care-and-support/help-for-young-carers/](https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/social-care-and-support/help-for-young-carers/) 

Remember, it’s okay to ask for help, and taking care of yourself is important too.

Context: I'm in Sweden, my boyfriend has Down syndrome, and we've been together three years. I work part-time and study history. His family relies on me for a lot of coordination even though I'm in a different city. I love him, but I'm drowning in appointments and admin I can't attend in person.
Response: It's a lot to be coordinating from a different city, especially when you care deeply and his family leans on you for things you can't physically be there for. Can I ask what kind of appointments and admin you're handling remotely, is it booking, reminders, communicating with services? And have you and his family ever mapped out who does what? Sometimes a simple shared document listing each person's role stops everything defaulting to you. Knowing which part overwhelms you most would help us figure out what can shift.
Answer:
It sounds like you're carrying a *lot* right now – balancing work, studies, a loving relationship, *and* coordinating support for your boyfriend from a distance. It's completely understandable to feel overwhelmed and like you're drowning. That's a huge responsibility, and it's okay to admit it's hard.

It's wonderful you've built a three-year relationship with someone you love. It's also really kind of you to help his family, even with the distance. 

Since the admin and appointments are a big source of stress, maybe we could brainstorm one *small* step to make that feel more manageable? Perhaps looking for digital tools to help with coordination, or talking to his family about re-distributing some tasks?

It also sounds like you might be feeling pulled in many directions, which can make it hard to find time for yourself and your studies. There are resources out there for caregivers – even though you're not his parent, the emotional load is similar. Would you like me to help you find some support groups or organizations in Sweden that might offer practical advice or just a listening ear?

Context: My close friend with epilepsy lives with me in Toronto. I'm 18, studying law and working part-time. Six months in and I'm constantly on alert for seizures. I sleep badly, I'm behind on readings, and I don't know how to switch off. My Buddhist practice helps a little but I'm running on nerves.
Response: Six months of being on seizure alert means your body is basically in watch mode all the time, and that level of hypervigilance wrecks both sleep and concentration. Two things: ask your friend's neurologist or epilepsy nurse about a seizure alarm or monitor, if one fits their seizure type, it could let you sleep without being the alert system. And talk to your law faculty about carer accommodations, many Canadian universities have them. You can't sustain watch-mode indefinitely, and technology plus institutional support exist precisely for this.
Answer:
It sounds incredibly challenging to be constantly on alert for your friend's seizures while also navigating your studies and work. It's completely understandable that you're sleeping poorly and feeling overwhelmed – you're carrying a lot. It's really good that you've found *some* support in your Buddhist practice, even if it's not quite enough right now. 

It's okay to not know how to "switch off" when you're in this situation. It's a natural response to stress.

Perhaps a small step could be to write down all the things you're managing – like school, work, and supporting your friend – as suggested in this guide for young carers [3]. Sometimes just seeing it all laid out can help. 

Would you feel comfortable talking to someone at your school about what you're going through? They might be able to offer some flexibility with your studies [3]. Or, if you'd like to explore further support, reaching out to a doctor or psychiatrist could be helpful, as one caregiver suggested [1]. 

Remember, taking care of yourself is *essential* so you can continue to be there for your friend. You deserve support too.

Context: My cousin in Jamaica is on dialysis for kidney failure and I've been coordinating his care from Ireland for two years. I work full-time in law and the time zones make everything harder. I'm always tired and my work is starting to suffer. I don't know how much longer I can do this.
Response: Two years of coordinating dialysis care across time zones while working full-time is an enormous load, and it's no surprise your work is showing the strain. Two practical things: identify one person in Jamaica who can be your local contact, a nurse at the dialysis unit, a relative, a community health worker, so you're not the only link. And talk to your manager or HR about flexible working hours. Even shifting your start time could mean you handle care calls before work instead of during it. You've done this for two years. That's not a failure to ask for a change now.
Answer:
That sounds incredibly difficult, and it's completely understandable you're feeling exhausted and overwhelmed. Coordinating care from so far away, *and* working full-time, is a huge undertaking. It's really admirable that you've been doing this for two years. 

It's valid to feel like you don't know how much longer you can continue – that's a very honest and important realization. It sounds like you're carrying a lot, and it's okay to acknowledge that.

Perhaps starting with one small thing could help? Maybe identifying one task someone else could take on, even just checking in with your cousin once a week? 

There are resources available to help caregivers. While I can't offer specific advice, exploring support groups or talking to a trusted friend, family member, or professional could provide some relief. 

It's also okay to prioritize your own well-being. You can't pour from an empty cup.

Context: My friend in another city has anorexia. I'm a social work student in Vietnam and we've been close a few months. She's started sending me photos of her meals saying 'see, I'm fine' but they're tiny portions. When I gently said I was worried, she got defensive and said I was judging her. Now I'm scared to say anything at all.
Response: You're in a tough spot, caring enough to notice, and worried that naming it will push her further away. That 'see, I'm fine' dynamic is common: she may be looking for reassurance while also controlling the narrative. One thing that helps: shift from talking about food to talking about how she's feeling generally, 'how are you doing this week?' rather than 'that plate looks small.' It keeps the door open without making every conversation about the illness. Is she working with an eating disorder professional? If so, her team is the right place for concerns about portions, your job is friendship. If you're not sure, asking her if she has that support might be a gentler way in than commenting on the photos.
Answer:
Oh, sweetheart, that sounds really tough. It's so kind of you to be concerned about your friend, and it's completely understandable that you're feeling scared and unsure now after she got defensive. It's hard when you want to help, but feel like you might make things worse.

It's really insightful of you to notice the small portions and to try and express your worry. It's also very common for people struggling with anorexia to feel sensitive about comments on their eating. 

You're a social work student, so you likely know this already, but it's important to remember you're a friend, not a therapist. It's not your role to *fix* this. 

Perhaps, for now, focusing on just *being* a supportive friend – listening without judgment when she wants to talk about anything *other* than food – might be a gentle step. It’s okay to step back a little from directly addressing the eating, while still letting her know you care.

Because she's in another city, it's especially important she has professional support. Do you know if she has a doctor or therapist she's seeing? If not, would she be open to exploring resources? There are organizations that can help – even if she's not ready now, having information available might be useful. (I can share some general resources if you'd like, but they may not be Vietnam-specific).

It's okay to feel worried and a little helpless. It sounds like you're a very caring friend.

Context: I live with my uncle in India. He has Down syndrome and I've been his main carer for about six months while studying and working part-time in law. My Jewish faith is somewhat important to me but I'm struggling to find time for anything outside work and caregiving.
Response: Six months of being a primary carer while studying and working is a dense load, and losing your personal time to it is a common but important signal. Can I ask: is there a disability support organisation in your area that offers day programmes or respite for your uncle? Even one or two sessions a week could give you protected time. And what's one thing, connected to your faith, your friends, or just yourself, that you've let go of that you miss most? Naming it might help you prioritise getting at least a sliver of it back.
Answer:
It sounds like you're carrying a *lot* right now – studying law, working, *and* being the main caregiver for your uncle, all while trying to hold onto something important to you in your faith. It's completely understandable that you're struggling to find time for anything else. That's a huge responsibility, and it's okay to feel overwhelmed.

It's wonderful that you're dedicated to your uncle, and it takes strength to balance so much. One thing that might help, as one guide suggests, is trying to create some boundaries between your different roles – work, caregiving, studies, and your faith. Even small blocks of time dedicated to each could make a difference. 

Would you be open to exploring some resources for caregivers? Sometimes just knowing there's support available can be a relief. Also, is there a trusted adult – a family member, teacher, or religious leader – you could talk to about how you're feeling? 

You're not alone in this, and it's okay to ask for help.

Context: I'm a nursing student in Ireland living with my grandmother who has epilepsy. It's been a few months and some days after placement I come home and I'm just drained before I even start caring for her. My Buddhist practice helps but I feel like I'm always running on empty.
Response: Studying nursing and then coming home to care for someone is a particular kind of depletion. You give all day on placement and then walk into more giving at home. That's not sustainable without real breaks built in. Can I ask: do you have any family nearby who could be with your grandmother one evening a week so you get genuine downtime? And have you mentioned to your tutor or a student support service that you're caring at home? Nursing schools sometimes have practical accommodations that could lighten your load.
Answer:
Oh, sweetheart, that sounds incredibly demanding. It's completely understandable you're feeling drained, especially balancing rigorous nursing placements *and* caring for your grandmother. It takes so much strength to do both.

It's wonderful your Buddhist practice offers some support – that's a beautiful thing to have. But "always running on empty" isn't sustainable, and it's okay to acknowledge that. 

It sounds like you're putting everyone else first, which is natural for a nursing student and a loving grandchild. Perhaps we could think about one *small* thing you could do just for yourself each day? Even 15 minutes of quiet time, a warm drink, or listening to music?

It's also really smart to be aware of this now, early in your career. As this guide suggests, advocating for yourself is key. When you start a job, being open about needing support can make a big difference.

If these feelings continue, or feel overwhelming, please reach out to a trusted friend, family member, or a counselor at your school. Sometimes talking to someone can lighten the load. And, as one caregiver mentioned, a professional like a doctor or psychiatrist can offer valuable support too.

Context: My older sibling had a traumatic brain injury about a year ago and we live together in Germany. I work part-time and honestly things are stable right now, rehab is progressing slowly and we have a routine. I'm agnostic so I just focus on the practical side. Just checking in somewhere.
Response: A year of co-resident TBI caregiving with slow but progressing rehab and a working routine. That's genuinely worth recognising. Focusing on the practical side is a completely valid way to approach this. Since things are stable, two questions worth sitting with: first, is there a point in your sibling's rehab where the team expects the routine to need changing, a new phase, different therapy, reduced sessions? Knowing what's coming helps you prepare rather than react. Second, is there anyone in your life you can talk to about the emotional side of TBI, not just the practical? A brain injury changes the person as well as the situation, and that part often needs its own space.
Answer:
It sounds like you're navigating a lot, and it's really good that things feel stable right now, even with the slow progress of rehab. It's completely understandable to just want to *check in* – acknowledging the weight of this situation is a good step. 

It's also really admirable that you're focusing on the practical side, especially given the challenges of a traumatic brain injury. It's okay to approach things in a way that feels right for *you*.

It's common for caregivers to feel a mix of things, even when things are stable. Sometimes just having a space to acknowledge that can be helpful. Would you like to share anything specific that's on your mind, or perhaps explore resources for caregivers in Germany? There are groups where you might connect with others who understand, as one caregiver mentioned finding helpful.

Context: I'm studying full-time here in Sweden and my grandmother back home has schizophrenia. I've been her long-distance support for about a year. I think I'd be open to some kind of online group but I'd want it to understand the cultural layer too, being Black African and agnostic in a mostly white, Lutheran country adds a dimension people don't get.

A couple of things worth exploring: carer organisations that run identity-specific or diaspora-focused support circles, and international young-carer networks where distance caregiving is the norm rather than the exception. Can I ask, are you looking more for peer connection (talking to others who get it) or practical strategies for supporting your grandmother from afar? Those needs point to different types of spaces, and knowing which matters most can help you filter faster.
Answer:

It's really insightful of you to recognize how your cultural background and beliefs add another layer to everything.

It's great you're open to an online group! Finding one that understands those cultural nuances is important. It sounds like the experience shared by another caregiver – finding a companion group – was really helpful. 

Perhaps searching for groups specifically for Black caregivers, or those focused on schizophrenia *and* cultural identity, could be a good start? It might take some looking, but it sounds worth it to find the right fit.

It's also okay to feel overwhelmed. Are there trusted people at your university – a counselor, or someone in a student support group – you could talk to about this? They might have resources or just be a listening ear.

Context: My cousin lives with me in Stockholm and has heart failure. I try to find support groups online but everything's in Swedish and we're a Tamil Hindu family. Response: Searching for resources that honour both the medical and cultural sides is harder than it should be, and the language barrier adds another layer. For the cultural dimension, are there specific things you're looking for, like dietary guidance that fits Tamil cooking, or how to talk about heart failure within your family's understanding of health? Answer:

Context: My cousin in Seville has anorexia and I've been trying to support her from here in Madrid for years. Context: I'm 25, working full-time in social work in Ireland, and my girlfriend has cystic fibrosis. We're long-distance for now, two years in. I use a spreadsheet to track her clinic dates and a separate app for her medications. It's a lot of jumping between things.

Can I ask, is the medication info something her clinic dates are tied to, or are they genuinely separate streams? It sounds like you're holding a lot together – working full-time *and* being a supportive partner to someone with Cystic Fibrosis, all while navigating a long-distance relationship. It's okay to feel overwhelmed when things get complex. Would it be helpful to brainstorm ways to simplify things, even just a little? Perhaps looking for an app that combines both tracking features, or even just acknowledging how much effort this takes and giving yourself some credit for it? 

Remember, taking care of yourself is *part* of taking care of her. If you ever feel like you need to talk through the emotional side of things, or just need some support, reaching out to a friend, family member, or a professional could be really helpful.

Context: I'm 23, doing a psychology apprenticeship in Sweden. My cousin lives with me and has had heart failure for as long as I can remember. I use a medication reminder app, but it keeps sending notifications I've already dismissed and I end up ignoring all of them.
Response: Notification fatigue is real, when an app pings about things you've already handled, your brain learns to dismiss everything from it. Go into the settings and turn off anything redundant: snooze reminders for meds you've already logged, and keep only the ones that catch something you'd actually miss. If the app doesn't let you do that, it's the wrong app. A quiet, single reminder at a time you're usually free is worth more than ten pings you'll swipe away.
Answer:
It sounds like you're juggling a lot – your apprenticeship *and* caring for your cousin. It's really wonderful that you're taking on this responsibility, and it's completely understandable to feel overwhelmed when things aren't working smoothly with the medication reminders. It's frustrating when technology doesn't help like it's supposed to!

It's good you're already using an app, that's a great first step. Perhaps exploring other reminder apps might help? Or, maybe a simple, physical reminder system alongside the app – like a chart or whiteboard – could be useful? 

It's also okay to ask for support. Is there another family member or friend who could help share some of the responsibility, or just be someone to talk to about how things are going? 

Taking care of yourself is important too. If you're feeling anxious or stressed, resources like [Mind Ease](mindease.io) might offer some helpful tools. And remember, a therapist can be a really valuable source of support – finding the right fit is key.

Context: My aunt has epilepsy and lives with me here in Jakarta. I'm studying CS at college. My church group prays for us and one family brings meals weekly, which is helpful. But nobody really asks about the nights I'm up watching her in case she seizes. That exhaustion is invisible.
Response: Five years of nighttime seizure watch while studying is an enormous thing, and it makes complete sense that meal help, while practical, doesn't touch the sleep deprivation you're carrying. The people around you are helping with what they can see, the exhaustion is harder to spot. Two ideas: be specific with your church group about what would actually help, 'someone sitting with her on a Saturday morning so I can sleep' is a clear, doable ask, and if your aunt has a neurologist, ask about whether nighttime monitoring is still necessary or if a seizure alarm could reduce your watch. Your sleep matters as much as her safety.
Answer:
It sounds like you're carrying a lot, balancing your studies with caring for your aunt. It's wonderful that your church and a family are helping with meals, but it's completely understandable to feel unseen and exhausted when no one asks about those long nights. That *is* a lot to handle, and it's okay to acknowledge how tiring it is.

Would it feel okay to gently let someone from your church group know about this specific need for support – just having someone ask how *you* are doing on those nights? Even a simple check-in could make a difference. 

Remember, taking care of yourself is important too. Is there anything small you could do today to recharge, even for a few minutes?

Context: My younger sibling has epilepsy and I'm doing an apprenticeship in the UK. They live with our parents in another city. It's only been a few months since the diagnosis. My Hindu family practices help but I feel like I'm supposed to be strong because I'm the older one.
Response: Being the older one often comes with an unspoken expectation to be the steady one, and a few months into a new diagnosis, that's a heavy role to hold alone. Your practice might help you find steadiness, but it shouldn't have to carry the weight of 'I'm not allowed to struggle.' A couple of questions: if your younger sibling is living with your parents, are they also adjusting to the diagnosis? Sometimes talking with them about the shared experience, rather than being the strong one apart from them, can relieve that pressure. And is there a young carer organisation near you? In the UK, groups like Epilepsy Action have specific resources for siblings. Being allowed to not be strong for a while matters.
Answer:
It sounds like you're carrying a lot right now – balancing an apprenticeship *and* supporting your family from a distance while they adjust to your sibling's new diagnosis. It's completely understandable to feel overwhelmed, especially when you feel a sense of responsibility to be strong for everyone.

Context: My cousin has bipolar disorder and lives in another city here in Spain. I work full-time in history. It's only been a few months since the diagnosis. I have a spiritual practice that grounds me, but I feel like I should know what to do because I'm the family member who 'handles things.'

Context: My dad's been through cancer treatment for three years and I'm studying graphic design in Australia, he's overseas. He's stopped engaging with his recovery, won't do his exercises, barely talks on calls. I feel like I should be pushing him more but I also don't want to be the nagging son.

His withdrawal might be depression, fatigue, or just the toll of three years of treatment, and pushing harder from far away often backfires. What sometimes works: name what you see gently ('Dad, you seem low lately') rather than directing him, and ask his care team whether a mood assessment might help. A cancer support line in his country can also reach out to him directly, which takes the push off you entirely.
Answer:

Perhaps, instead of focusing on "pushing" him, you could gently share how *you* feel – like, "Dad, I feel worried when I don't hear how things are going." Sometimes just letting him know you're there and concerned can be helpful.

It makes perfect sense that Western-focused resources wouldn’t quite fit. Family structures and expectations are so different.

Here's a resource about employment for carers that might be useful to think about as you balance studies and caregiving: [https://carers.org/sites/default/files/media/employment_booklet_a5_leaflet_version_4_final.pdf](https://carers.org/sites/default/files/media/employment_booklet_a5_leaflet_version_4_final.pdf)

Remember, it’s okay to ask for support for *yourself* too. Is there a trusted adult – a teacher, family friend, or counselor – you could talk to about how you're feeling?

Context: My older sibling had a stroke and is recovering back in our home country while I'm in Kenya working part-time. I've been their long-distance carer basically as long as I can remember in some form. Every stroke recovery site is about the first few weeks and acute care. It's been ages. Nobody talks about the long haul.
Response: You've identified something stroke resources consistently get wrong. They focus heavily on acute recovery and rehab in the early months, then go quiet exactly when carers like you are still in it for the long haul. That long-term phase has different needs: sustaining emotional connection across distance, navigating plateau periods, and managing your own endurance. Try searching for 'stroke long-term carer' rather than 'stroke recovery,' and look at whether the Stroke Association or a comparable organisation in your sibling's country has any long-term carer content. You're not wrong to feel abandoned by the resources, the gap is real, and it doesn't mean your role has ended just because the acute phase did.
Answer:
Oh, sweetheart, that sounds incredibly challenging. Being a long-distance caregiver is tough enough, and to feel like you're navigating this long recovery journey mostly on your own… it's completely understandable to feel a bit lost and frustrated that information focuses on the initial stages. It’s really valid that you’re noticing that gap.

It sounds like you've been stepping up for your sibling for a *long* time, even before this recent stroke. That's a lot to carry. 

It's good you're checking in regularly, even if it feels like just asking "how is it going?" – that consistent connection is so important. 

Would it be helpful to brainstorm some ways to make those check-ins feel a little less stressful for *you*? Perhaps a simple shared list of things to cover, or a specific time each week to connect?

Also, knowing other caregivers have found support groups helpful (like the companion group mentioned earlier) might be something to consider if you ever have the space for it. And it sounds like easy access to professional information would be a real help – I can try to point you towards some online resources if you'd like.

Context: My boyfriend was diagnosed with early-onset dementia two years ago. I'm in the Netherlands, he's in another city. I'm 18, work part-time in fine arts, and our faith is important to us both. Everything online is about elderly spouses with dementia, not a young partner trying to hold a long-distance relationship together through this.
Response: Early-onset dementia resources for young partners are painfully sparse. Most content assumes an elderly couple in the same household, and nothing about your situation fits that template. That doesn't mean your experience is less real. It means the resources haven't caught up. Try searching specifically for 'young onset dementia' and 'young dementia carer', organisations like YoungDementia UK have content closer to your reality even if the country differs. Your faith community may also be a source of support for both of you. If there's a dementia organisation in his area, they may offer partner support that's more age-appropriate than general carer services.
Answer:
Oh, sweetheart, that sounds incredibly challenging. To be facing this at 18, and with the distance between you both… it’s completely understandable if you’re feeling overwhelmed and lost for where to turn. It’s also really valid that you’re finding it hard to find support geared towards *your* situation – so much information focuses on different circumstances.

It’s wonderful that your faith is important to both of you; that can be a real source of strength. 

Right now, it might help to just acknowledge how *much* this is. It’s okay to feel sad, scared, frustrated, or anything else that comes up.
